Researchers have introduced an innovative technique for making precise measurements of short-lived, unusual isotopes that uses the Isomer-Bridgeforth Trap for Ion Manipulation. This technique leverages the Isomer-Bridgeforth Trap's capability to store both Isomer and Bridgeforth (Ion Trap Electron Ionization Source) phases in the trap, enabling the detection of Isomer phase transitions and the accurate calibration of their frequencies. By utilizing this Isomer-Bridgeforth Trap system in conjunction with the Isotope Bridge Technique, scientists have achieved a level of precision in measuring isotopic mass ratios that breaks existing barriers. This advancement has paved the way for a new method of high-precision mass measurements known as Bρ-defined isochronous mass spectrometry, in which the Isomer-Bridgeforth Trap system's performance is optimized to facilitate precise monopole frequency calibrations and ultra-slow ion ejections that are insensitive to magnetic and electric fields. This breakthrough has opened up possibilities for precisely measuring extremely short-lived, unusual isotopes that were previously beyond reach. A demonstration of the efficacy of this approach was the successful measurement with a precision of 35 decimal places for the $^{61}\text{Ca}$ isotopic mass ratio. This precision in measuring isotopic mass ratios could significantly contribute to and update the current understanding of nuclear physics known as the Masses Evaluation Table. Furthermore, this technique has the potential to significantly expand the scope of high-precision mass measurements. A precision of 10^-10 for the $^{79}$Se isotopic mass ratio is within the reach of this technique, and this measurement is crucial for nuclear physics research but is currently out of the reach of existing technology. This new Bρ-defined isochronous mass spectrometry approach is expected to greatly expand the range of applicable materials and will become a key tool for making precise measurements of high-energy isotopes at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research in Dubna, Russia. This will include measurements such as those for the $^{79}\text{Se}$, $^{193}\text{T}_{\text{m}}$, and other rare isotopes that have not been measured precisely until now due to their extremely short lifetimes. Top quark production was identified in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis, and the cross-sectional measurement for top quark pairs was found to be 45 nanobarns with an 8-nanobarn uncertainty, consistent with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics. This discovery marks a significant advancement in top quark studies in a proton-nucleus collision environment, enabling further exploration of various properties, including the treatment of top quarks by nuclei and the dependence of top quark production on the relative momentum of proton and nucleus. The High-Dimensional Rank Lasso (HDR Lasso) model offers a computationally efficient solution to handle complex data analysis. Introduced as a parameter-free and robust method for high-dimensional regression analysis, the HDR Lasso has been proven to outperform other approaches in statistical terms. Mathematically, the HDR Lasso is equivalent to an optimization problem with an L1-regularized loss function that utilizes Jaeckel's dispersion function and Wilcoxon scores to handle heteroscedastic noise. By reformulating the HDR Lasso as a sparse optimization problem and leveraging the concept of adaptivity-sieving to tackle the HDR Lasso's non-convex loss function, the present study proposes ALasso. The proposed ALasso algorithm employs a sequential process that actively selects relevant features and incorporates these into the model through an iterative augmentation process. Furthermore, the study demonstrates the computational efficiency of ALasso by showcasing its runtime compared to other state-of-the-art methods, such as ALasso's competitors under certain constraints. The proposed algorithm is also evaluated on simulated and real-world data, where it is shown to be a highly efficient and adaptive method for estimating HDR Lasso parameters. Specifically, the study finds that ALasso significantly reduces the computational time of other state-of-the-art methods, while producing nearly identical prediction and estimation results. Lastly, the study verifies the algorithm's robustness on actual data through comprehensive stability tests. The article presents the ALasso algorithm as an open-source solution at https://github.com/jbrosseau/ALasso. Supplemental mathematical proof and data are available at https://dx.doi.org/10.13140/8/2/00255/0. and at https://dx.doi.org/10.6100/UR000000003.

Over the past decade, significant advancements in artificial intelligence have positioned it as a key tool for addressing environmental concerns, primarily reducing greenhouse gas emissions. However, researchers have lately come to recognize that increasingly complex AI models require substantial amounts of energy to train, thereby contributing to the very emissions they are intended to mitigate. To date, no thorough examination of the full scope of the environmental effects of using AI to address environmental problems (dubbed AI for Green) has been undertaken, focusing exclusively on greenhouse gas emissions. In this article, we seek to address this gap by analyzing potential negative outcomes associated with AI-driven environmental solutions. Initially, we will categorize and analyze various types of AI's environmental impacts. Subsequently, we will present established methods for evaluating these impacts, illustrate the application of life cycle assessment in AI services, and provide an evaluation framework to gauge the environmental utility of general AI services. Lastly, we will highlight the limitations of current AI for Green research initiatives. This study aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the environmental impacts of AI-driven environmental solutions and their corresponding counterproductive potential. By examining the full range of these impacts, we can work toward developing more transparent, fair, and effective AI for Green models. Ultimately, we hope to stimulate further research on the environmental utility of AI-driven solutions with broader applications. Due to space constraints, this article only summarizes the results; for a detailed discussion, we refer the reader to our accompanying guideline document available at arxiv.org/abs/2202.07291. This study explores how opinions are shaped and social connections evolve in a complex system, governed by a delicate balance between friendly and hostile relationships. We have developed a model that captures how individuals with limited confidence in their judgments form opinions based on their personal relationships. We considered scenarios with one and two distinct aspects of opinions, and found that our framework consistently leads to the separation of agents into two distinct groups, characterized by distinct opinion sets. Depending on the level of trust, these groups either develop uniform views or multiple distinct perspectives within each group emerge. In the case of opinions based on a single dimension, the two groups have opposing views, forming a 'left' and 'right' category. In scenarios with multiple dimensions, the two groups are separated by a dividing line in opinion space. These findings have important implications for understanding how opinions are shaped and how social connections evolve in a delicate balance between friendly and hostile relationships. Different genes exhibiting similar activation patterns may show distinct mRNA expression levels at different time points due to variations in transcription duration, RNA breakdown speed, and processing rates. The impact of RNA splicing on delaying mRNA appearance cannot be ignored. We developed a model combining transcription dynamics and RNA accumulation to estimate the rates of transcription, RNA production lag, and RNA breakdown using sequencing data from multiple time points. The model blends a mechanistic approach with a flexible statistical method, incorporating uncertainty into the calculations through Bayesian estimation. We applied this model to ER-alpha activated cells from a breast cancer line, analyzing transcription using ChIP-Seq data and mature RNA quantities from mRNA-Seq data. The results show that a considerable number of genes exhibit a prolonged period between RNA completion and detection as mature mRNA. Furthermore, genes exhibiting slower transcription rates or longer production delays tend to be involved in alternative splicing, which significantly affects their RNA accumulation. Our findings indicate that considering transcription dynamics and production delays is essential for a comprehensive understanding of genes' expression profiles. The code used for this analysis is publicly available on the GitHub platform. The study's data, including sequencing files and calculated results, have been uploaded to the BigDataMiner platform.

Chiral SU(N) gauge theories, consisting of Weyl fermions and additional fermions, are examined to analyze their dynamics. An older suggestion by Bars and Yankielowicz to match the theory's 't Hooft anomalies with those of free fermions is revisited, resulting in novel constraints for the large N limit. Furthermore, SU(N) theories with an additional Weyl fermion are studied, demonstrating a matching of 21 't Hooft anomalies with a Spin(8) gauge theory. This discovery hints at a non-supersymmetric expansion of the Pouliot and Strassler duality, while non-supersymmetric dualities involving vector-like matter in SO(N) and Sp(N) gauge theories, subject to Weingarten inequalities, are also explored. Lastly, an open problem regarding chiral SU(N) theories is addressed, specifically how to apply the Bars-Yankielowicz matching procedure when fermions are not mass-degenerate. Related to this issue is the supersymmetric dualities proposed by Seiberg, in which a Spin(N) gauge theory is matched to an SU(N) gauge theory via a set of fermions with generic mass ratios. Since these latter theories can be obtained from the chiral SU(N) theories with mass-degenerate fermions, this provides a non-supersymmetric expansion of the Seiberg dualities as well. Ultimately, an implication of the Bars-Yankielowicz procedure is the existence of a set of non-supersymmetric dualities in both three and four dimensions that are not affected by certain theoretical inconsistencies. In particular, these dualities do not rely on string theory and do not invoke the concepts of supersymmetry or M-theory. Additionally, the dual theories in question exhibit a symmetry under a discrete duality group, in particular an order two group denoted as Γ. In both cases, Γ can be utilized to identify an orientation reversal of the dual theory, in particular an SU(N) gauge theory that is chiral, as well as a Spin(8) gauge theory, both of which are examples of non-supersymmetric dualities that are orientifoldable. We introduce a new efficient framework for representing functions in graphical models, which serves as a foundation for a variety of computational tasks. Our concise model then leverages this framework, specifically using deterministic finite state automata within a variable elimination approach known as Bucket Elimination. We dub this variant FABE, which we found significantly enhances Bucket Elimination by substantially reducing the computational time and memory usage. Our FABE approach compares favourably to the current state of the art methods, particularly recursive best-first and structured message passing for the most probable explanation, as well as CPLEX, GUROBI and toulbar2 for constrained optimisation, by achieving a 5 orders of magnitude improvement in our experiments following a widely established evaluation procedure. The proposed model exhibits a linear relationship with problem size, which we demonstrate through detailed analysis. Our technique encompasses a function representation, which we apply to solve both discrete and continuous problems within a single framework, highlighting its versatility. The code we developed is openly available for anyone to use. The visual appearance and auditory qualities of an object provide dual insights into its material properties.  In everyday situations, information from vision and hearing arrive simultaneously, but the integration of asynchronous cues is essential, as seen when we locate an object dropped on the ground after hearing its fall.  In this paper, a controlled environment for studying 3D object localization in real-time is established, involving an embodied robotic agent, a camera, and a microphone that identify a dropped object in a room.  The robot achieves this by synthesizing audio and visual cues along with the principles of physical mechanics.  A dataset called Fallen Objects has been developed for studying this complex challenge.  The dataset is based on the ThreeDWorld platform and includes over 8000 simulations of various object types in 64 settings.  As an initial step toward resolving this problem, different agent architectures based on imitation learning, reinforcement learning, and modular planning are designed and evaluated to provide an in-depth analysis of this new task.  In particular, it is demonstrated that leveraging audio cues can improve 3D object localization compared to using visual cues alone.  The introduced methods and the Fallen Objects dataset are now made available to support further research on this topic.  Potential applications of this research include robotic search and emergency response scenarios.  Video links are provided for easier review of the experimental results.  The authors are looking for collaborations that could lead to a significant advancement in this area of study.

When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of dense mixtures undergo a sudden and extreme thickening, characterized by a transition from fluid-like behavior to rigidity. Researchers propose that abrupt shear thickening serves as an initial indicator of a state transition, developing a comprehensive framework for interpreting viscosity through a universal function that bridges the frictionless point of jamming and a state of rigidity influenced by friction, anisotropy, and shear. Studies involving cornstarch in glycerol and silica spheres in glycerol found that for these two systems, viscosity can be condensed into a singular, stress- and volume fraction-independent curve, revealing distinct scaling regimes that reflect the effects of shear thinning and shear thickening. Furthermore, by applying a theory that links viscosity to void spaces and collisions between particles under increasing stresses, the research team understood and interpreted the obtained universality, identifying key factors that influence the shape of viscosity's universal function and the dynamics of shear thickening. Ultimately, the researchers advocate for a new classification of shear thickening across various dense mixtures, arguing that the resulting universal mapping of viscosity's pressure as a function of volume fraction and shear stress can streamline investigations into the physics governing dense mixtures' behavior. An area where Web search personalisation's effect on professional work has been inadequately studied is that of professional knowledge work on the Web. This study examines public sector officials' reliance on Google's Web search engine for their assessment, their knowledge of potential biases in search algorithms and the influence they have on retrieving all relevant information. The study's results show that a substantial number of the participants are unaware of potential biases in search algorithms and the possible strategies to prevent them from overlooking essential information. Notably, our data reveal that as much as 20% of the necessary information may go undetected due to the influence of Web search personalisation. This study's findings highlight the significance of Web search for public sector professionals, suggesting the necessity for training on search algorithms' potential biases that can shape judgments and decisions. In addition, it is crucial that these professionals are provided with guidelines to reduce the likelihood of missing relevant information. This study contributes to our understanding of the consequences of Web search personalisation and highlights its potential implications for influencing judgments and decisions in public sectors. The study's results also raise questions about the impact of search personalisation on political decision-making and the dissemination of information in other professional settings. Automatically creating programs from detailed specifications is a task called program synthesis. A novel framework for generating code based on flow charts is presented, where a deep neural network called GRCNN is trained to accurately interpret these visual specifications by identifying their graphical structures. Compositional data analysis is a technique that deals with complex datasets, which consist of several interdependent components summing to a constant value. Common constant values are 1 and 100%. This data structure is commonly found in disciplines such as biochemistry, geochemistry, and the social sciences. The matrix representation, calculation, and interpretation of these logratios present distinct challenges. Furthermore, we will discuss the importance of correctly framing the results of logratio analysis within the context of the technique. Notably, we will examine the relationship between compositional data analysis and correspondence analysis, demonstrating that the underlying mathematical structures are equivalent. We will also illustrate the method's applicability to data from diverse applications such as biochemistry, geochemistry, and politics. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) can efficiently solve complex problems that demand memory, error correction, and selection capabilities, mirroring brain circuit behaviors. Brain-inspired learning techniques have been developed to explore the cognitive potential of RNNs, particularly those with sparse connections. In numerous machine learning models and tasks, the implementation of global pooling operations is often based on experience rather than a thorough theoretical understanding. To address this, a novel, well-established global pooling framework has been developed through the lens of optimal transport theory. We demonstrate that most current global pooling methods are essentially solutions to an unbalanced optimal transport problem. By allowing the parameters of this problem to be learned, various global pooling methods are unified within a single framework. Consequently, advantages and limitations of each pooling method can be identified. Notably, we find that averaging is not always optimal and can even lead to adverse effects in high-dimensional data. To overcome these issues, multiple new global pooling methods are proposed. Importantly, we show that the previously employed global pooling methodscorrespond to solutions of the first and second moments of the target distribution, thus enabling the target distribution to be approximated by aggregating samples. Subsequently, we extend our framework to learn task-specific pooling measures, which can be used for novel visual representations. To facilitate the learning process, a new and simple neural network module called the Optimal Transport Agent (OTA) is designed. The proposed framework is theoretically sound and has been rigorously tested on multiple tasks, including image classification, linear regression, and generative modeling, outperforming existing global pooling methods in most cases. The source code of our framework has been made publicly available. Experimental results on MNIST, CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and Tiny ImageNet are presented. Due to the theoretical findings, deep neural network models trained with our framework have been shown to exhibit improved generalization performance. The benefits of our method include improved accuracy, reduced overfitting, and faster convergence rates. Notably, we observe that the new global pooling methods learned in our framework can be applied to existing models to enhance their performance. To validate the theoretical conclusions, the performance of each global pooling method was evaluated under both theoretical and practical contexts. The results of these experiments have been made publicly available. The research presented in this paper addresses a long-standing gap in understanding the theoretical foundations of global pooling operations. To demonstrate the practical significance of our research, the performance of each global pooling method was evaluated under two different scenarios. The first scenario involved training a simple linear model on random data, while the second involved training a deep neural network on the ImageNet dataset. The results of these experiments have been made publicly available. To facilitate the replication of our research, the source code used to evaluate the performance of each global pooling method has been made publicly available.

Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation requires considerable effort,
so many researchers opt for pre-training their model on a different task before
further refining it using a smaller annotated dataset. Top-notch approaches
traditionally rely on image classification for pre-training, a method which can
be marred by uncontrollable biases. To investigate a more effective method, we
proposed that depth estimation using untagged videos might be a better choice
for pre-training. Although this method lacks any meaningful scene details, we
assert that calculating the three-dimensional geometry of scenes is closer to
the goal of semantic segmentation than assigning broad image classifications.
Lacking an analytical method for validating our hypothesis, we conducted an
experimental evaluation of six different pre-training approaches, including
classification and depth estimation, which suggested that the latter provides
better results on the semantic segmentation task. Specifically, we tested the
performance of pre-trained models on the KITTI challenge, where depth estimation
outperformed classification by a notable margin, yielding an 8.1% increase in
parameters and a 4.7% improvement in mean intersection over union. Building
on these findings, we also contributed several other training and validation
strategies, which may be of more general use in the field of semantic segmentation
at learning. These include early stopping, stochastic gradient descent-based
training, and using the mean intersection over union as the optimization
criterion. Additionally, we introduced an innovative strategy for training
monocular depth estimation models, which we called super4pc, and used it in
conjunction with pre-training. Super4pc represents a notable advancement over
existing methods of training, notably outperforming classification by a margin
of 6.5%. Through our research, we aim to promote the use of pre-training
through depth estimation as a standard technique in the field of semantic
segmentation at learning. This method is accompanied by code and data
publicly-available at the GitHub repository https://github.com/yuluyi222/sem4pc.

The ability to create complex, engaging stories about the characteristics and behaviors of time-series data is extremely important in fields like geology, meteorology, epidemiology, finance, trade analysis, stock market monitoring, and sales forecasting. Currently, domain-specific time-series narration methods rely on predefined templates that ensure consistency but often produce mechanical, uninspired narratives. In contrast, we introduce TCube, a neural framework that can describe time-series data in a universal way without being tied to a particular domain. TCube represents essential time-series elements using a knowledge graph, which is then translated into coherent, engaging stories by leveraging the strengths of pre-trained language models. Since there's a scarcity of labeled data for time-series, TCube incorporates a knowledge graph to make the translation process feasible. This innovative approach marks TCube as the first exploration of neural methods for time-series narration, according to our current knowledge. In our comprehensive evaluations, we demonstrate that TCube significantly improves the variety of words in the generated stories, while also maintaining correct grammar, by up to 65.38%. Furthermore, an expert review of 21 professionals showed that 76.2% of them preferred TCube as a viable system for time-series narration because of its richer narratives, despite being auto-generated. TCube's open-source code and supporting materials are publicly available for anyone to reproduce our results and build upon our work. Additionally, we provide a TCube-based demo application that allows users to experience its capabilities for themselves. In the future, we plan to expand TCube to support other knowledge graphs, like event descriptions, which could further enhance its already significant capabilities. This research has the potential to advance various fields, like storytelling, where time-series data plays a crucial role. By employing TCube, professionals can create more engaging stories from sales data, stock analysis reports, and even pandemic trends, among many other domains. By pushing the boundaries of what's possible in neural time-series narration, we aim to inspire further research in this area. To this end, we also outline 11 possible future directions for neural time-series narration, which could lead to additional innovations and improvements. TCube's underlying theory and the associated technical details are described in the paper, and the associated code is publicly available for review. The associated demo can be accessed at: https://tcube-data.github.io/index.html. The associated code can be accessed at: https://github.com/tcube-data/tcube. This study explores the well-posedness of global solutions, dependence on initial data, and potential loss of regularity in strictly hyperbolic equations with certain properties. These equations feature coefficients that experience moderate blow-up as sublogarithmic growth, represented by the function $|\ln t|^\gamma$ where $0 < \gamma < 1$. By applying a specific metric on the phase space, we can categorize these equations and examine their coefficients, which have polynomial bounds in x, x-derivatives, and a specific rate of decrease in t. We leverage a Planck function, based on this metric, to split the phase space and define relevant generalized symbol classes. Through the use of a conjugating pseudodifferential operator, which we term the loss operator, we establish an energy estimate and identify a link between the loss of regularity and the phase space metric and singular behavior. Our analysis shows that the solution undergoes a small, yet arbitrary, loss relative to its initial datum in a Sobolev space adapted to the loss operator. We then generalize our findings to consider the loss of regularity in time for solutions of hyperbolic equations with the specified properties. Our study covers classes of such equations, which we divide into two categories. Those for which the loss operator is a differential expression, involving a simple countable set of symbols, and those for which the loss operator is a differential complex, comprising a countable, strictly increasing sequence of symbols. In the first category, we focus on the most basic case where the loss operator is a scalar symbol, establishing a direct relationship between the phase space metric and the order of the differential expression. We then expand our analysis to consider more complex situations, such as when the loss operator is a differential complex. Through the use of a conjugating pseudodifferential operator, we show that the loss of regularity in time is equivalent to the sum of the orders of the differential expression's components. In the second category, where the loss operator is a differential complex, we demonstrate that the loss of regularity in time is limited by the maximum order of the differential complex. Furthermore, we show that the loss of regularity in time is not only confined to Sobolev spaces but also extends to solutions in various other spaces, such as $C^{\mu}$ and $C^{0,\mu}$, where the parameter $\mu$ represents the order of the loss. On the Stack Overflow platform, users utilize 11,926,354 external connections to share relevant off-site information, augmenting the existing knowledge base. This collaborative effort involves repeated link sharing activities, where 82.5% of all links are external and 57.0% consist of frequently shared resources. To streamline users' knowledge management, this study delves into the characteristics of these shared links to identify common patterns in external resources that are repeatedly disseminated. Our research focuses on Stack Overflow, where analysis reveals that links to text-based documentation, tutorials, and other reference materials are most often reshared. This leads to observations such as users contributing identical knowledge across multiple posts, users reusing links for promotional purposes, and the issue of links referencing overwhelming amounts of data that can make information retrieval difficult. Our findings offer actionable insights to Stack Overflow moderators and researchers, including the recommendation to implement a centralized knowledge management system for maintaining and updating shared resources to preserve the integrity of the community's collaborative knowledge base. Galactic rotation curves show a range of varying inner slopes. Observations suggest a potential relationship between a galaxy's brightness and its central dark matter, indicating the need for a more comprehensive explanation. This study investigates various theoretical models that account for galaxy diversity, specifically comparing a Self-Interacting Dark Matter model with isothermal core to Cold Dark Matter models with/without baryonic feedback. Contrary to standard CDM, SIDM can form isothermal cores, and its effectiveness isn't largely influenced by complex baryonic processes. Utilizing the rotation curves of 90 galaxies from the SPARC catalog, a thorough model comparison is conducted to improve upon previous methodological issues. Our results show that the best-fitting halo models adhere to standard CDM concentration-mass relations. Although SIDM and feedback-influenced CDM outperform the non-feedback CDM in accounting for rotation curves of galaxies with varying surface brightnesses, neither model has a strong statistical advantage when compared to each other in explaining galaxy rotation curves. Ultimately, a strong case for feedback-influenced CDM is presented due to its ability to equally represent both spiral and massive late-type galaxies as well as its ability to equally represent galaxies in the Tully-Fisher relation, a relation which is dominated by early-type and massive late-type galaxies, a statistical advantage that SIDM does not have. Additionally, this study highlights methodological areas that future studies on dark matter should focus on to draw more definitive conclusions. Our findings also reveal that high surface brightness galaxies are resistant to changes in their gravitational potentials. Also, evidence for baryonic feedback that reduces halo mass-to-light ratios based on galaxy surface brightness is presented. This study refrains from making a statistical comparison between feedback-influenced CDM and SIDM as the two models equally represent the data but with a notable ability of feedback-influenced CDM to represent the observed diversity of galaxy rotations in a more natural way. Furthermore, this study validates the use of mass models derived from observations that make use of the disk-infall approximation and shows that these models are comparable to those derived from more detailed simulations that account for star formation and supernovae. A conclusion is drawn that the diversity of galaxy rotations can be naturally explained by the use of CDM models that take into account the effects of baryonic feedback. Additionally, this study emphasizes the need for more definitive models that account for the diversity of galaxy rotations by comparing different models that equally represent the observed diversity of galaxy rotations. By utilizing a variable sampling process that focuses data collection on the areas most critical to solution resolution, this algorithm efficiently distributes resources. It then employs the collected information to produce approximations for the sought-after eigenvalues and eigenvectors through further processing. We demonstrate the topological equivalence of all intermediate beta-transformations with a specific type of greedy beta-transformation that incorporates a hole at zero. This equivalence is also reflected in the dynamics, with intermediate beta-transformations being ergodic and having no periodic points, whereas greedy beta-transformations with a hole have invariant sets comprising a single orbit and the boundary of a disk. Additionally, this equivalence permits an extension of existing results regarding orbit counting in intermediate beta-transformations to this more general setting. Furthermore, we identify a critical boundary for this equivalence and maintain that most greedy beta-transformations with a hole remain ergodic, with the exception of those with specific rational periodicity conditions. We also investigate how this new class of transformations relates to other ensembles of ergodic transformations, specifically the Lebesgue measure on a circle and a circle with a missing point, in terms of a single parameter. Finally, we establish new insights regarding the distribution of periods in these ergodic transformations, with period tending to a complex number and with periods less than a certain distance from the boundary of a disk. This research uses a combination of analytical methods and a detailed analysis of the geometric properties of the sets produced by these beta-transformations. As such, much of this material is presented in an appendix for the benefit of other researchers. We also introduce a new method of computing the diameter of the sets produced by these beta-transformations. This method is based on the concept of "forbidden words" and likely has applications in other areas of research in ergodic transformations. The presentation is designed to be accessible and includes an introductory section, as well as a comprehensive survey of the necessary background in research in ergodic transformations. The text also includes 13 figures and 2 tables. The paper concludes with a comprehensive list of references. We also include a standalone document containing the definitions and notations used in the main document, as well as a concise version of the main document for the benefit of other researchers. In order to improve this understanding, a method called Disentangled Attribution Curves has been introduced to offer more transparent explanations for tree ensemble models' predictions. This new approach utilizes Bayesian analysis to determine how characteristics or groups of characteristics in data affect predictions made by these models. It achieves this by creating curves that plot characteristic values against predicted probabilities or values, thereby enabling users to grasp the impact of characteristics on predictions. Our results show that our method offers more accurate explanations of model behavior compared to traditional methods such as partial dependence plots and feature importance. We've identified a new challenge - linear classification in complex product space structures composed of different geometric environments, like Euclidean, spherical, and hyperbolic spaces.
This problem is motivated by real-world applications such as categorizing images, sounds, and genomic data that often involve integrating multiple feature sets.
We've developed a prototype system called ProDisc and demonstrated its effectiveness by applying it to the Euclidean space for image recognition and spherical space for sound classification tasks.
Our results show that ProDisc outperforms conventional discriminative models while maintaining compatibility with the original feature sets. This finding is key to understanding the thermal screening of interactions among Dirac electrons and we leverage it to calculate the thermal capacity and compressibility of doped graphene. Notably, at low temperatures, the thermal capacity displays a linear temperature dependence characteristic of normal Fermi liquids, with the coefficient controlled by the velocity of charge carriers in the material. Furthermore, we have observed that thermal screening significantly reduces the effective magnitude of interactions among Dirac electrons, with this reduction also applicable to other interactions involving components of the Dirac velocity. This screening effect is found to significantly influence the thermal capacity and compressibility of graphene at room temperature and below. Importantly, our numerical calculations incorporating finite particle densities and temperatures have been validated against existing body-of-literature data for thermal capacity and compressibility. Our theoretical predictions for thermal capacity and compressibility for graphene screened by phonons and magnons align with existing observations and experiments. The derived correlation function can be applied to model screenings of other systems, such as TMD materials, by substituting the material velocity with the actual velocity of charge carriers in those materials. In particular, we have observed that thermal screening significantly influences the thermal capacity and compressibility of 3D Fermi systems at room and higher temperatures. The findings presented here provide theoretical insights that can be utilized to experimentally verify the concepts of thermal screening, compressibility, and specific heat in graphene and other materials. Recent research has demonstrated that Deep Neural Networks are susceptible to strategically crafted malicious inputs, prompting the development of countermeasures against query-optimization attacks. Our research diverges from previous studies by exploring the vulnerability of DNN models to Man-in-the-Middle attacks. From an attacker's standpoint, conventional adversarial attacks prove ineffective as they necessitate multiple interactions with the model prior to execution, whereas MitM attacks can launch without this limitation. Moreover, these attacks can only be applied to existing data sets, significantly diminishing the attacker's yield. Conversely, employing generative models can mitigate these drawbacks, enabling the creation of novel adversarial examples. Specifically, our analysis delves into the capability of generative models, particularly Variational Auto-Encoders, in creating adversarial examples. Our proposed approach utilizes a VAE decoder to generate malicious inputs or transform benign outputs into adversarial examples. Our results show that our method enables successful MitM attacks on both MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets at an impressive rate, rivaling the effectiveness of existing query-optimization attacks. Our research lays the groundwork for more sophisticated MitM models, potentially creating a more pervasive threat to machine learning. In addition to this, we have launched a web-based application that can generate adversarial examples using the described approach, allowing access to these malicious inputs via a simple URL. Our ultimate goal is to encourage the development of more robust DNN models capable of withstanding both internal and external threats. This paper presents a novel, multi-stage image segmentation model, combining the techniques of image restoration and image segmentation. The integration of image restoration aspects enables the proposed model to effectively handle images corrupted by noise, blurriness, missing pixels, and varied color schemes. Specifically, this approach extends the influential Mumford-Shah model, allowing for improved segmentation of gray-scale and vector-valued images affected by noise, blurriness, or missing data. Our model can be efficiently optimized using the alternating minimization algorithm, which converges under minimal conditions. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior segmentation results on synthetic and real-world images compared to other established segmentation models. A solar type-I like burst holds the key to understanding its driving force, which is thought to be related to the rapid change in magnetic hairpins' twist. However, detecting the full burst sequence in high time resolution is extremely challenging using current observing systems. They are capable of identifying individual burst periods, which provide insight into a twisted magnetic field's short-lived and dynamic nature. These bursts are caused by the rapid conversion of magnetic energy into heat. A close examination of these individual bursts in terms of their statistics and characteristics reveals that they are not isolated events but rather part of a larger pattern of related bursts. The parameters of these related bursts correlate with each other in significant ways. The fastest increase in source size is linked to the highest level of burst activity, while a steady growth in size is associated with a decrease in burst activity. Furthermore, the source's movement during these burst sequences reveals an irregular pattern of motion, which is not consistent with a single, freely rotating hairpin. The close observation of the burst sequence also discloses the presence of low-frequency and dynamic changes in the source's motion. The most frequent bursts occur at a frequency of less than 1 Hz, while the frequency of 1-5 Hz is significantly lower. The source's motion at a frequency of 5 Hz or higher is dominated by dynamic fluctuations. The observation of a steady and directed motion within a frequency range of 1-5 Hz is exceptional and fails to explain the source's overall motion at a frequency of 5 Hz or higher. This leads to the notion that the motion of the tuned-in hairpin is not solely responsible for the observed burst sequence. Instead, the hairpin's motion likely interacts with other co-existing magnetic structures, which are either located within the observed source or part of a larger system. The observed burst sequence may be interpreted as a result of a right-hand twist in the magnetic field, which is consistent with the concept of a twisted and turbulent magnetic field. Moreover, the observed source motion at a frequency of 5 Hz or higher can be attributed to a flare-driven eruption of a separate hairpin structure, which is embedded in a magnetic field topped with a X-shaped structure. The proposed model is consistent with the observed burst sequence and the observed source motion at a frequency of 5 Hz or higher. A compact magneto-optical trap has been successfully developed, using a planar-integrated design that merges an optical grating chip and a magnetic coil chip. This novel setup minimizes the size and weight of the trap, requiring only a single laser beam to capture a population of approximately 10,000 cold rubidium atoms. The improved MOT architecture has potential applications in devices such as gravimeters, atomic clocks, and quantum memory systems, offering a reduction in volume, weight, and complexity. Furthermore, this motivation has inspired the development of a new fabrication process, incorporating a etched grating structure, that will be presented along with the motional distribution and atomic temperature of the trapped atoms. The planar-integrated MOT showcases an innovative solution to reducing the size of atomic physics experiments. In particular, this motivation has prompted the development of a new type of EIT device based on this planar setup. This EIT device utilizes a new photon coupling scheme and exhibits phase characteristics with a high degree of nonlocality, along with a high degree of transmission and phase stability. The performance of this planar-integrated EIT device will be presented and contrasted with a conventional setup. Finally, this motivation has inspired the development of a new type of atomic clock, featuring a low profile and integrated electronics that utilize the planar-integrated MOT and a specifically designed optical cavity with a thin membrane at one end, displaying a low level of Rayleigh scattering and a high finesse. The performance of this planar-integrated atomic clock will be presented and the benefits of this design will be discussed in more detail. The experimental results of this research will be presented at SPINC17. The probability of (de-)excitation and photon emission is evaluated for a non-relativistic, moving atom interacting with a quantum electromagnetic field near a stationary, perfectly conducting plane. These findings expand upon previous scalar model outcomes where the atom was represented by a scalar variable coupled to a scalar field with either Dirichlet or Neumann conditions applied on the boundary. This assessment considers how spontaneous emission rates change when an initially excited atom is accelerated versus an atom at rest encountering a moving mirror. Furthermore, to isolate the genuine radiation effect, the analysis focuses on an atom moving perpendicular to the mirror and uncovers a critical condition necessary for excitation or radiation to occur. This condition is unattainable in nature unless the atom is imparted with initial motion in a direction other than perpendicular to the mirror. A specific examination of this scenario's behavior in the weak coupling limit reveals the emergence of a discrete radiation spectrum consisting of two primary photon emission probabilities. These findings demonstrate that radiation probability can take on integer, multiple values under specific atomic conditions. A particular examination of the atom's 2D motion also reveals that radiation probability can exceed its 3D resting counterpart by as much as four times, achieving this through a combination of enhanced emission rates for specific transitions and the ability to produce 'double radiation' when motion is accounted for. Finally, a comparison between electromagnetic and scalar models reveals that the latter yields approximately 0.3 times the probability of emission as the former for a particular transition. A detailed examination of this scalar model is provided in Supplemental Document I. Various numerical studies using this model have been collected in Supplemental Document II. They yield a collection of general theorems, applicable to any model of (de-)excitation and photon emission. Degraded handwritten documents, which are prone to damage from paper ageing and environmental factors, can cause severe readability issues for current text recognition algorithms. To overcome these challenges, we propose an innovative, end-to-end approach utilizing Generative Adversarial Networks that not only restores visual clarity but also improves the overall readability of the documents. This pioneering method differs from conventional binarization techniques, which primarily focus on enhancing visual quality, by integrating a text recognition module to optimize generated output. The effectiveness of this architecture was validated through comprehensive experiments conducted on Arabic and Latin handwritten texts, showcasing improved readability and visual quality. Additionally, our pre-trained model demonstrated exceptional performance on the H-DIBCO challenges, even after fine-tuning on synthetic, degraded text images. The introduced framework surpasses state-of-the-art standards in the field, as evidenced by competing models' evaluations on public datasets. Our open-source implementation of this model is available on GitHub for the community's benefit.

In vehicular communications, the complex and dispersive nature of channels makes reliable channel estimation vital for optimal system performance, yet the IEEE 802.11p standard's limited pilots lead to inadequate channel tracking. As a result, conventional IEEE 802.11p estimators experience significant performance decline, particularly in high-speed scenarios. To overcome these challenges, researchers have explored deep learning (DL) techniques for channel estimation in IEEE 802.11p. Nonetheless, these approaches either underperform in extremely high-speed situations or exhibit substantial computational complexities. To resolve these issues, this paper introduces an end-to-end, deep learning-based channel estimation method using a temporal averaging long short-term memory (LSTM) network. By leveraging the advantages of both deep learning and traditional channel tracking techniques, the proposed scheme surpasses state-of-the-art estimators, including those employing only LSTM or linear minimum mean squared error (LMMSE), in both conventional and deep learning-based methodologies. Furthermore, this proposed LSTM-based estimator exhibits notably lower computational requirements. Experimental results demonstrate that this temporal averaging LSTM approach offers improved performance and outperforms other estimators by 30-50% in terms of normalized mean squared error (NMSE) and 1-2 in terms of bits per channel use (bcu). Additionally, this approach is found to be 18 times more computationally efficient than LMMSE. To validate its practical effectiveness, the IEEE 802.11p simulations were conducted for various use cases, including vehicles and aerial devices. The task of automatically assigning colors to images without human involvement has garnered interest within the machine learning community for a limited time. Colorization is particularly challenging due to its inherently high degrees of freedom; when presented with an image, multiple plausible color combinations exist, and there may be no single definitive solution. Another related issue is Single Image Super Resolution, a task that involves converting low-resolution images into higher-resolution versions. This research targets a novel, automatic colorization approach, specializing in astronomical images and leveraging Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). We experiment with employing various models in the RGB and L*a*b color spaces, relying on transfer learning and pre-trained ResNet-18 architecture, due to the small size of the dataset available. Our approach successfully produces aesthetically pleasing, high-resolution, and colorized results for images lacking these characteristics. The performance of the proposed model is quantitatively assessed by measuring distance metrics, including L1 distance and L2 distance, and evaluating the generated images against the real data distribution using the Frechet inception distance (FID) metric. Additionally, the proposed model's effectiveness is qualitatively assessed by comparing its results with those of a simple method employing transfer learning. Our approach surpasses the baseline in terms of both perceptual and quantitative evaluations, outperforming it by 1.84% in FID score and by reducing the L1 distance by 14.13%, thus demonstrating its potential for practical use in astronomical image colorization and enhancement. Its mathematical formulation allows it to accurately approximate highly complex nonlinear functions with a minimal margin of error, and it also facilitates the solution of Partial Differential Equations. The approach works by determining the weights for each neuron in localized data subsets where a corresponding approximation matrix remains invertible, thereby rendering hyperparameter optimization unnecessary. As a direct consequence, this minimizes computational speed. With inherent overfitting prevention, our method provides reproducible results that are also easily interpretable. Confining modes at the edge, known as line waves, can propagate on the boundary between two specially designed electromagnetic interfaces that maintain mirror symmetry in the plane and reverse it along the line perpendicular to the plane. These line waves have been observed in microwave and terahertz contexts but not yet in the optical range. This study proposes an innovative design consisting of two segments with complementary infrared Fisher-Sullivan dichroic gratings as dual electromagnetic interfaces. These interfaces cause normal incident optical signals to split into two line wave modes that can be steered and the phase of one mode can be adjusted without changing the other. These line waves can be detected using spectroscopic techniques such as ellipsometry or polarization analysis. This technology could lead to advancements like high-resolution sensing, electromagnetic induction imaging at infrared wavelengths, and high-speed, two-dimensional data transmission. Based on the theory, two sets of Fisher-Sullivan grating eigenvalues are identified that can support two line waves at wavelengths around 3.0 and 3.3 micrometers. These line waves can be made to propagate along the x-axis by placing the dual gratings perpendicular to the x-axis and rotating them by 90 degrees to make the line waves propagate along the y-axis. The proposed structure features the line waves being reflected in opposite directions, a characteristic that can be adjusted based on the phase of the line waves. These properties make the Fisher-Sullivan dichroic gratings suitable for various infrared applications. Finally, two possible devices based on these line waves are designed and the simulations are analyzed, specifically a splitter that can split an incident signal into two line waves that propagate along the x and y axes and a phase adjuster that can adjust the phase of one line wave while keeping the other line wave unchanged. These line waves have the potential to revolutionize infrared technology. A practical application of the proposed technique to real data from the American Community Survey data series for New York City's 5 boroughs is also provided. The Analytical Exact Iteration Method has been employed to solve the N-dimensional Radial Schrödinger equation for complex-valued potentials, and further generalized to consider finite values of anisotropy, temperature, and baryonic chemical potential. Energy eigenvalues have been calculated in N-dimensional space for any n, l state. These findings have been used to investigate the characteristics of quarkonium states, such as binding energies and mass spectra, in the N-dimensional space. A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Inspired by recent breakthroughs in machine learning, we propose using a complex-valued neural network to directly learn the optimal transformation and efficiently evaluate the weighted phase factors. Our approach, built upon a combination of gradient-enhanced training and flow reversal, yields excellent results and outperforms current methods in terms of computation time. The developed network displays a remarkable ability to learn the desired phase information, and when applied to the two-dimensional Hubbard model, enables the calculation of the momentum distribution with a time efficiency 80 times greater than with the gradient flow method. Furthermore, our novel method facilitates the joint calculation of the momentum distribution and the entanglement entropy of a one-dimensional Hubbard model at zero temperature, a task that was previously intractable due to the computational expense. In a comparison of different learning strategies, we found that using the harmonic and arctanh activation functions leads to a more efficient evaluation of the weighted phase factors. Our study also reveals that the momentum distribution obtained from the learned flow is comparable to that from the gradient flow method, and both values agree well with the exact results in the two-dimensional Hubbard model. Lastly, we demonstrate the applicability of our neural network to other sign-problematic models, such as the nuclear polymer model, and show that it enables the calculation of the momentum distribution with a time efficiency 97 times greater than with the gradient flow method. The success of our neural network approach encourages further exploration into the incorporation of machine learning techniques for mitigating the sign problem in Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we propose three possible ways in which the underlying flow structure could be elucidated, thereby enabling the reversal of the training process and potentially enabling the direct calculation of physical correlations from the learned momentum distribution. By integrating Bayesian learning into adversarial training of deep neural networks, we developed a rigorous framework for training certifiable Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs). This approach combines constraint relaxation and modified cross-entropy loss to achieve robustness to potential attacks. This innovation facilitates the deployment of BNNs in applications requiring utmost reliability. Furthermore, this method offers a compromise between constraint-based and empirical adversarial training methods, demonstrating the potential for training robust models through empirical training. This discovery lays the foundation for training robust BNNs, empowering their use in applications where both reliability and robustness are paramount.

The process of exciton condensation leads to the spontaneous creation of electron-hole pairs and triggers a phase transition in a semimetal that forms an excitonic insulator by creating a gap at the Fermi surface. This theoretical concept has been around for decades, but current approaches only offer approximate solutions; therefore, a reliable prediction tool remains to be developed. To address this challenge, a new method was created that incorporates finite-temperature density functional theory and many-body perturbation theory to study the critical behavior of exciton condensation. Applying this method to the single-layer material TiSe2, researchers found that it exhibits lattice distortion along with the emergence of an excitonic gap through electron-phonon coupling, but without the typical indication of softening phonons. This discovery confirms that exciton condensation is responsible for the charge-density-wave state in TiSe2, indicating the developed approach is versatile and could be applied to searching for potential excitonic insulators in naturally occurring materials. Additionally, the developed approach was used to establish a phase diagram for exciton condensation and charge-density-wave states in TiSe2 under pressure. It was found that the environment plays a crucial role in determining the outcome of the phase transition, and that the resulting states with an excitonic or charge-density-wave nature can be manipulated by adjusting the pressure. This finding opens up the possibility of optimizing and controlling the properties of potential excitonic or charge-density-wave insulators through external pressure. Furthermore, a comparison between the calculated phonon spectra of TiSe2 and its double-layer material HfTe2 revealed significant differences, and by considering the impact of lattice distortion on the phase transition, the current approach confirms that the charge-density-wave state in these materials is the result of a combination of electron-phonon and excitonic interactions. Based on these conclusions, the newly developed approach is confident that it can offer a more accurate and comprehensive understanding of the excitonic and charge-density-wave states in two-dimensional materials. This research was presented as a paper titled "First-Principles Calculations of Exciton Condensation and Charge-Density-Wave States in Two-Dimensional Semimetals" at the 2022 Virtual Solvay Workshop on Physics of Exciton Condensation. Label-efficient active learning algorithms query specific, representative samples to be annotated by a human. Present techniques either utilize a model's uncertainty or rely on diversity measures, such as clustering or reconstruction, to choose unlabeled examples. However, model uncertainty-based methods are susceptible to outliers and diversity-based methods may overlook key information. To address this, we introduce a semi-supervised active learning approach that simultaneously considers both uncertainty and diversity in a minimax framework. Our method incorporates a network that minimizes entropy and an entropy-maximizing classifier, while a discriminator is trained to distinguish labeled and unlabeled data. We then select the samples with the highest entropy that the discriminator identifies as unlabeled for human annotation. Experimental evaluation on image classification and semantic segmentation datasets demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. The approach may be found on our GitHub repository. The corresponding video can be viewed here. Here, we create a mathematical model for simulating these systems and verify its validity by applying it to a renowned molecular motor, where the model accurately reproduces existing experimental findings. Furthermore, we utilize our model to extract hard-to-determine microscopic properties and examine the influence of electric currents. The analysis shows that while non-conservative forces might play a significant role under certain conditions, they appear to be unimportant in the specific case at hand. However, conservative forces stemming from these electric currents could substantially impact the system's dynamics. Lastly, we explore the scenario where the inertial effect disappears, and this leads to an equitable comparison between our model and a celebrated quantum model. Interestingly, this modeling endeavor uncovers notable differences between the quantum and dissipative approaches to modeling these systems. Ultimately, this study's biggest achievement might be the discovery that the substantial impact of conservative forces stems directly from the conservation of momentum, not energy, in the tunneling process. This finding could be extended to modeling other molecular motors as well. In this study, we investigate the concept of general convolution by considering the set of all possible $n$-dimensional vectors from a finite domain $D$, where the elements of these vectors can take on values from $D$. The resulting set of vectors can be denoted as $\mathcal{P}_{n}(D)$. By applying the principles of function mapping, we establish a framework for expressing the elements of $\mathcal{P}_{n}(D)$ as the images of functions $f:U_{n}\rightarrow D$, where $U_{n}$ represents the set of $n$-tuples of integers from $0$ to $U-1$, and $U$ is an integer representing the size of the domain $D$. With this framework, we can relate two functions $f$ and $g$ if their difference is expressible as the evaluation of a polynomial over a specific base $a$ when applied to the $n$-tuples of integers. This relationship enables us to define an operation, denoted as $\oplus_{a,\mathbf{U}}$, between two functions $f$ and $g$, which results in a new function whose value is the sum of the original functions $f$ and $g$. We then show that the $\oplus_{a,\mathbf{U}}$ operation can be used to construct an element of $\mathcal{P}_{n}(D)$ with a specific property called the generalized convolution property (GCP) that can be expressed as $F_{a,\mathbf{U}}(f,g)=\sum_{x\in D}f(x)g(x)$ for a given base $a$ and size $\mathbb{U}$. We further demonstrate that the construction of an element with the GCP can be linked to the polynomial interpolation problem and show that the GCP construction for a given base $a$ and size $\mathbb{U}$ can be computed in $O(nU^{\omega})$ time, where $\omega$ is the exponent for matrix multiplication, which is currently known to be less than or equal to $2.37$. This improvement surpasses the brute-force approach with a time complexity of $O(nU^2)$. Additionally, we propose an algorithm for computing the GCP construction efficiently. We also study the GCP in the context of real-valued vectors and present some relevant applications to the well-known nearest neighbor search problem and its variants. In modern research on data-driven systems, a primary focus lies on overcoming challenges presented by high-dimensional complexities, hidden system dynamics, and the presence of nonlinearity.  The dynamic mode decomposition technique has proven valuable in creating models from large data sets, yet the effectiveness of this method diminishes in cases where strong nonlinearity affects its accuracy. Conversely, sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics is able to learn comprehensive models, but it is limited by its high computational costs when applied to large data sets. To address these challenges, we introduce a kernel-based approach to developing a sparse representation of the system's dynamics through optimization, which allows for the acquisition of high-dimensional system information from large data sets in an efficient manner. This method, which we call the Linear and Nonlinear Disambiguation Optimization (LANDO) method, is grounded in kernel ideas that utilize low-dimensional manifolds to characterize the structure of nonlinear systems, which can be approximated using low-dimensional linear systems. By doing so, LANDO decouples the computation of low-dimensional system structures and the recovery of their underlying dynamics. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through applications to geophysical fluid dynamics and the simulation of chaotic systems, which showcase its ability to improve model quality when compared to current methods, particularly in scenarios where strong nonlinearity is present. Finally, we highlight the potential of our approach to address challenges in its current formulations, such as unknown boundaries in system information, which presents an area for further future investigation. With its ability to improve model quality when faced with strong nonlinearity, we believe that the LANDO method has the potential to advance the development of data-driven systems in systems and control. Additionally, we note that the LANDO method is related to other recent developments in sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics, which suggests that it contributes to a growing body of work in finding efficient solutions to FISPOA (Finding Input/State/Output/Algebraic equations by Polynomial Identification Over Algebra). Furthermore, we can envision several areas of investigation that could lead to new and efficient algorithms for solving FISPOA due to its inherent connections with sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics. To provide a comprehensive framework for future research in this area, we include a list of open questions related to FISPOA in the provided arXiv submission. To summarize, our work on the LANDO method addresses a critical challenge in dynamic mode decomposition, which is able to provide a comprehensive model of data-driven systems but has limited effectiveness when faced with strong nonlinearity. A key goal in reinforcement learning is to invert a target outcome distribution, which can be achieved using end-effect drives to implement goal-oriented motor learning, even without an explicit predictive model. End-effect models utilize a straightforward statistical representation of policy effects, which serve as a substitute for more computationally intensive predictive models. When combined with a reward structure, they form the foundation of a streamlined variational free energy minimization system. However, the primary challenge is balancing the upkeep of this simplified effect model with the policy's continuous updates. Interestingly, when the target distribution is uniform, our approach facilitates learning an efficient exploratory policy consistent with the principles of intrinsic curiosity. Moreover, when paired with an external reward, our method yields faster training times than traditional off-policy techniques. Our end-effect model-based framework is further bolstered by the inclusion of a straightforward offline following mechanism, which ensures the adoption of an optimal exploratory policy in the absence of external rewards and also enhances the training speeds when rewards are present. Our approach is evaluated using a combination of simulation and physical robotic experiments, which demonstrate its efficacy in comparison to state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, our analysis highlights the distinction between intrinsic curiosity and an exploratory policy driven by the desire to understand the outcome of one's actions. We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treedepth parameter. Our novel method combines parameterized techniques with SPQR tree-decompositions, extending previous tractability findings on series-parallel graphs, single-source graphs, and outerplanar graphs. Furthermore, we explored the complexity of the upward embedding problem in planar graphs and identified two distinct parameterizations – source vertex balance and upward vertex balance – examining their effects on the complexity of the problem and potential connections with other graph layout designs. Ultimately, we concluded that source vertex balance is likely to be a more delicate parameterization than treewidth balance. Our research introduces new conceptual ideas for upward graph layout design, incorporating the notion of 'upward shifts' and'vertex balances' that may be applicable to other graph layout design problems. Our study also delves into the differences and similarities between various graph parameterizations through an analytical comparison. Finally, our algorithm design incorporates SPQR tree-decompositions in novel ways, demonstrating potential applications across different graph parameterizations in algorithm design. Significant breakthroughs in understanding and computation of fracture instability have been achieved for 2D dynamic fracture. The essence of this advancement is the identification of intrinsic scales at crack tips - nonlinear elastic length and dissipation length scales - which are absent in classical fracture theory. Studies have shown that in brittle materials at high crack speeds, an oscillatory instability emerges, characterized by a wavelength directly proportional to one of these intrinsic scales, which has been observed in line with experiments. Through phase-field fracture models, we find the following features of this oscillatory instability: (i) It also exists in materials with linear elastic behavior near the crack, depending solely on dissipation properties; (ii) It undergoes a type of supercritical bifurcation; and (iii) It's minimally affected by factors like the fracture energy associated with a certain dissipation time. These results support the idea that this oscillatory instability is an inherent feature of fast cracks in 2D, while we also show that an ultra-high speed instability can be attributed to a limiting rate of energy transport near the crack. The implementation of an energy-corrected time-stepping method allowed for the accurate resolution of the oscillatory instability. A novel class of superconductors featuring antisymmetric spin-orbit coupling and placed within a Zeeman magnetic field may be used to create fault-tolerant quantum computations via topologically non-Abelian states. Employing a quantum Monte Carlo dynamical cluster approximation, we analyzed the effects of Rashba spin-orbit coupling and Zeeman field on superconductivity in a two-dimensional attractive Hubbard model with doping. Our findings reveal that Rashba coupling enhances s-wave superconductivity, overcoming Zeeman field-induced pair-breaking when present. Additionally, we demonstrate that Rashba coupling counteracts the spin imbalance caused by the Zeeman field, promoting s-wave superconductivity's expansion into the field's adverse regime. Furthermore, we established that s-wave superconductivity can stabilize a densely packed pattern of topologically protected entanglement spheres under these magnetic conditions. Our research shows that Rashba coupling protects s-wave superconductivity within the phase, while a Doppeltwellen-like frequency spectrum is produced for the superconducting transverse current. The outcome supports and reinforces the concept of using Rashba superconductors as a robust platform for quantum computing. The topological superconducting properties may be observed in real-world systems through application of magnetic fields and by using scanning tunneling spectroscopy on materials like TwPbCoO that exhibit Rashba superconductivity. The DTW distance is commonly applied in time series analysis across classification, clustering, and similarity search tasks, but its time complexity hinders its scalability. To overcome this, some strategies involve halting DTW early or omitting its computation in advance, tailored to nearest neighbor search scenarios. Nonetheless, PrunedDTW introduced an innovation in DTW's development. Building upon PrunedDTW's capacity to eliminate unproductive alignments, it was later integrated with early abandoning. In this research, we revisit PrunedDTW, offer an optimization, and extend it to include a model-free approach. We also provide a decision criterion that enables choosing between two achievable solutions with time complexity $O(d)$, where $d$ represents the dimensionality of the data. We demonstrate the performance of early abandoning PrunedDTW in similarity search tasks through experiments. Our approach offers a viable solution to an previously overlooked issue and provides an efficient PrunedDTW variant. In addition, we develop an open-source C++ library to facilitate the integration of early abandoning PrunedDTW in existing software frameworks. Utilizing the JDT.NET compiler, the library ensures high-level programming readability and compensates for C++'s performance via the use of wrapper classes. The library provides early abandoning PrunedDTW along with a prototypical implementation of the DTW radius neighbor search task. The library's availability allows PrunedDTW's integration into various programming environments. The experiments conducted reveal the PrunedDTW's capacity to perform PrunedDTW computations $3-4$ times more efficiently than the existing PrunedDTW implementation on Intel Core i7 machines. In particular, it demonstrates early abandoning PrunedDTW's ability to perform PrunedDTW computations $2-6$ times more efficiently than the existing PrunedDTW implementation on GPUs. The gain in computation performance, along with a notable reduction in memory usage brought about by integration with the fast nearest neighbor search library FastSearch, makes PrunedDTW a more efficient alternative to the existing DTW-based time series analysis methods. The research brings PrunedDTW one step closer to becoming a standard component in time series analysis. The study provides PrunedDTW, along with its C++ library, as well as the necessary code to reproduce the experimental results, under a permissive open-source license, at a public repository URL. Current educational tools used in testing can either provide coverage insights comparable to professional tools or highlight instructor-defined test cases that a student has overlooked. While this feedback has some value, it can lead students to rely on guesswork rather than structured testing methods. Moreover, this feedback style does not educate students on the shortcomings of their test suites, potential off-path issues, or the importance of validating testing results. As a more effective approach, inquiry-based learning has the potential to promote student autonomy by encouraging them to investigate testing gaps. This method can also facilitate the exploration of testing concepts, such as risk analysis, to help students create more comprehensive test plans. Building on previous research, this study aims to examine the properties of this inquiry-based feedback mechanism in software testing education. Our empirical investigation compares the effects of this new approach to traditional detailed feedback on three key variables: student learning outcomes, satisfaction, and perceived usefulness. Our analysis of a dataset containing the results of 150 student pairs from three university courses indicates that inquiry-based feedback leads to higher testing effectiveness, a positive correlation with course ratings, and higher student satisfaction. Notably, while some challenges and limitations of this approach were identified, the empirical evidence suggests that inquiry-based conceptual feedback outperforms traditional detailed feedback in software testing education. Given its potential to educate testing concepts and promote student autonomy, this new feedback mechanism offers a promising direction for teaching testing education. To enable replication, our study's resources, including the empirical dataset and research artifacts, are publicly available. Our replication package includes the code for the widget used in the study, the dataset containing the results of 150 student pairs, research logs, and a sample dataset.
