Previous research has suggested the use of SRAM-based TRNGs for extracting entropy from SRAM arrays. As these SRAMs are commonly employed in specialized or general-purpose chips for storing program data or binary instructions, SRAM-based TRNGs can provide high-quality randomness without affecting system performance. Nevertheless, existing SRAM-based TRNGs have several drawbacks, including high energy consumption, prolonged delay, and limited scalability. In contrast, we propose an SRAM-based TRNG that offers high randomness efficiency and concurrently enables significant reductions in energy consumption and processing time. Our approach involves under-scaling the SRAM supply voltage to induce statistically uniform bit fluctuations, which are then captured and converted into genuine randomness. In comparison to traditional SRAM-based TRNGs that operate at nominal voltage, TuRaN, our proposed solution, demonstrates improved energy consumption and processing time. For example, on the C432 benchmark circuit, TuRaN showcases a 3.27x decrease in energy consumption, a 2.45x decrease in processing time, and yet still maintains the same high randomness efficiency. Furthermore, TuRaN can be scaled up for extracting randomness from SRAM-based arrays while continuing to provide high randomness efficiency, enhanced energy efficiency, and accelerated operation times. To evaluate its reliability, we performed randomization tests on SRAM cells from the C432 and BDC105 benchmarks as well as a real-world microcontroller. Our results indicate that TuRaN successfully passes the NIST standards for randomness evaluation. In summary, TuRaN represents a reliable, high-quality SRAM-based TRNG solution that excels in randomness efficiency, underlies wide scalability, and offers performance improvements. As such, it has the potential to significantly impact the realm of SRAM-based TRNGs. The properties of thin films made from metallic transition-metal oxides can be significantly different from their bulk counterparts. In this study, we simulate a monolayer of strontium vanadate grown on a substrate to investigate the thickness-induced metal-to-insulator transition. We found that two different terminations lead to the same insulating behavior at equilibrium but exhibit distinct behavior when doped or subjected to a gate voltage. Through many-body calculations, we revealed various nonlocal fluctuations resulting from antiferromagnetic, ferromagnetic, stripe, and checkerboard orbital ordering instabilities. By considering the role of orbital degrees of freedom, we explain how these instabilities emerge and demonstrate how ultra-thin film reconstruction and changes to coordination polyhedra result in unique material properties. Additionally, we observed that several fluctuations coexist in different regimes and found that doping these films leads to distinct insulating, semimetal, and metallic states. Our research provides a comprehensive understanding of the complex physics of ultra-thin transition-metal oxides and sheds light on the material properties of prospective oxide heterostructures. \\

Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing.  Despite recent breakthroughs in deep learning, the task remains a challenge due to its complexity and practical applications.  A key limitation of deep learning models is their lack of generalizability on unfamiliar text types, often referred to as domain shift or section bias.  Researchers have explored various methods such as data augmentation and transfer learning to improve the performance of automated essay grading models.  In our study, we examined the effectiveness of data augmentation using transformer-based models through a comparative analysis of multiple approaches.  We found that using transformer-based data augmentation methods resulted in substantial gains in performance for our specific dataset.  Specifically, our results showed an 8.5 point improvement in our basic model and 11.5 point improvement in our fine-tuned model.  We also observed an 11.1 point improvement in our model that used BART data augmentation.  These findings have far-reaching implications for the development of accurate and scalable automated essay grading systems.  We also introduced an innovative and efficient method for generating parallel corpora through sentence aligning, as well as an adaptive training and tuning protocol that leverages a small set of human-annotated labels to achieve significant performance gains.  Our results from two large-scale datasets of middle and high school essays demonstrated the consistency and scalability of our approach.  Our work offers a solution to the longstanding problem of domain generalization in automated essay grading.  In addition to our contributions, we have made our code public to support the replication of our study.  We hope our findings will guide future research in this area.  We also present a comprehensive analysis of the results from an online pilot testing of our model. The resulting SL-MPSF method ensures system safety with fewer and less extreme adjustments to control inputs. Furthermore, we propose a specific variant of SL-MPSF that retains scalability and significantly decreases online processing requirements, which is the major drawback of traditional MPSF designs. The benefits of our safety filter design over state-of-the-art MPSF designs are demonstrated through numerical examples. Additionally, our method has been successfully applied to a real-world use case - parking tasks in a 2D environment - with experimental results showing its superiority over existing MPSF designs. Recent studies on large language models have demonstrated in-context zero- and few-shot learning abilities with promising results, yet their underlying dynamics are not yet fully understood. For instance, there is limited knowledge about how learning in-context changes when using varying training corpora. Our research aims to explore the influence of a pretraining corpus's origin and size on the performance of a Korean-centric model. Notably, we discovered four crucial findings: Firstly, a pretraining corpus's domain significantly affects the model's ability to learn in-context. Conversely, a pretraining corpus's size doesn't guarantee in-context learning to emerge. Furthermore, a pretraining corpus composed of multiple domains may facilitate the development of in-context learning, even when each domain doesn't result in in-context learning alone. Lastly, a pretraining corpus related to a downstream task may not always ensure a strong in-context learning performance for that task, particularly when it comes to the zero-shot setting, and that language modeling performance and in-context learning do not always correlate as one might expect. Ultimately, our research implies that a pretraining corpus's selection and optimization are necessary to achieve in-context learning with large language models. To address any concerns regarding overfitting that may arise from using a pretraining corpus, we observed that a fine-tuning approach on a downstream task also yields comparable or even stronger results. Our code and pre-trained models are publicly available for reproduction. This study extends the concept of in-context learning to a multi-domain context, and our data analyses provide insights that can be useful for future research in this area. Additionally, our findings may have practical applications in real-world natural language processing tasks. In the long term, our research may contribute to the development of more efficient methods for training large language models that can perform in-context learning and other advanced NLP tasks with ease. This work holds the potential for applications in task and slot filling, especially in settings that lack labeled data, and may be particularly useful for task-oriented dialogue models. As for potential technical applications of our research, it could be useful for developing models in scenarios where a limited number of training examples are available for a particular task, or where it is challenging to find a pretraining corpus that closely matches a downstream task. This model allows CN agents to share information and make decisions about resource allocation, thereby enhancing the efficiency of MNs. We showcase the efficacy of our model through a simple example, where CN agents dynamically adjust parameter settings to minimize energy consumption in MNs. This is achieved by CN agents varying their sleeping intervals to optimize circuit switched Aggregation Points (APs), thus reducing energy consumption in MNs. The potential of this model lies in its ability to automatically adjust CN agents to suit the needs of emerging MN applications, such as massive IoT connectivity scenarios, without human intervention. The objective of zero-speech synthesis is to create a vocabulary-independent speech system without transcription data, requiring the transformation of training data into acoustic units for test synthesis. This study explores identifying and modeling the fundamental acoustic units in speech, comprising both transient and steady-state regions. The transient regions are equivalent to consonant-vowel and vowel-consonant units, while steady-states include sonorants and fricatives. The speech signal is first segmented into CVC-like units based on a short-term energy contour and then grouped using graph clustering. The clustered units are initialized to include transient onset and decays, and steady-state rhyme components, and are subsequently rearranged into acoustic units in an HMM-GMM framework. The AU sequences are then used to develop synthesis models, and the effectiveness of the approach is demonstrated through the analysis of subjective and objective scores on the Zerospeech 2019 challenge database. The results show that acceptable quality speech synthesis at a low bit rate can be achieved with the proposed units. The proposed method is further compared to an acoustic unit-based method derived from transcription data, and the differences in performance are attributed to the inherent similarities and variations within the derived acoustic units. The study concludes by highlighting the challenges and limitations of the approach associated with the inherent complexities of speech communication. The proposed system performs best at a low bit rate, and is comparable to a transcription-based method at a higher bit rate. The use of the proposed units enables speech synthesis at a lower bit rate, and the derivation of acoustic units from short transcription data facilitates the synthesis of reasonable quality speech. The approach relies on short-term energy contours, and the transient and steady-state units, and is therefore suitable for low-bit rate speech synthesis. Optimizing multi-limbed robots' motion under posture and force constraints poses a challenging nonlinear optimization issue, often accompanied by extensive computation times. We've developed a multi-step optimization method incorporating data-driven linkages between stages to tackle these nonlinearities efficiently. Both cluster analysis and evolutionary strategies are applied to determine the specific parameters of McCormick envelope relaxations, allowing us to leverage learned constraints across preceding stages, thus yielding better performance, faster solution times, and more interpretable outcomes. Our planner was thoroughly tested and validated through a variety of walking and climbing experiments on a 10 kg hexapod robot. It successfully demonstrated the capability to walk on uneven terrain, climb 0.4 meter in 40 seconds, and save 20% time compared to standard methods. Moreover, the developed planner can generate a solution within 30 seconds that is only 5% longer than the optimal solution. In particular, the proposed planner outperformed a conventional method by reducing its optimisation time by a factor of 20 for a 0.4 meter climbing task, and also resulted in a solution that was only 3% longer than the optimal solution compared to being 20% longer with the conventional method. We have developed two overarching methods to quantify the manipulation of quantum states using probabilistic protocols constrained by specific quantum resource limitations.
Initially, we formulated a fundamental criterion for achieving a physical transformation between quantum states using a previously introduced resource metric.
This approach led to the discovery that the metric is not only necessary, but also sufficient, for one-shot resource conversion in various resource theories, essentially rendering more restrictive protocols unnecessary.
By employing this metric, we were able to refine the performance limits of one-shot and multi-copy probabilistic resource distillation protocols.
Concurrently, we introduced a comprehensive technique for calculating achievable probabilities in resource transformations through a series of convex optimisation problems.
This approach enabled us to precisely assess the trade-offs between probabilities and errors in the distillation of maximally resource-rich states.
Furthermore, we successfully demonstrated the efficacy of our methods in the analysis of quantum entanglement distillation. Importantly, our approach does not depend on the particular resource theory in question, making it universally applicable to diverse scenarios. The development of our methods necessitated a thorough examination of the boundaries between different regions of the metric space, which led to the discovery of some unexpected overlaps between these regions, specifically between the regions corresponding to classical, stochastic, and superdense coding. This analysis also facilitated the introduction of a novel decomposition of the state space and helped to establish a clear distinction between different types of states, such as superdense coding states and other types of states. Additionally, our approach led to a detailed assessment of the performance limits of multi-copy probabilistic protocols, essentially closing the gap between the theoretically achievable and existing performance limits in quantum entanglement distillation. The only limitation of our approach is that it is predominantly analytical, which makes it prone to scalability issues for complex states. To address this, we introduced a hybrid method that combines analytical and numerical techniques to facilitate a more efficient study of smaller, more complex states. This approach was demonstrated by achieving a significant improvement over the existing state-of-the-art protocols for single-copy and multi-copy resource distillation. Overall, our methods are anticipated to be valuable for the analysis of diverse resource theories and will likely have far-reaching applications in quantum information theory. Furthermore, our approach is expected to be beneficial for the development of various quantum technologies. This model was subject to two types of excitation - parametric in the vertical plane and a combination of parametric and direct in the horizontal plane. The position of the pivot changed over time, inducing these excitations. In the scenario of vertical excitation, the averaging method helped to establish stability boundaries for two steady-state solutions, whereas vertical and horizontal excitations led to system resonances identified through multiple scale methods, with results validated using exact numerical integration techniques. The application of this model to a situation where a person is carrying a cup of coffee illustrates how its loss of stability can lead to coffee spillage. This model's results show a strong correlation with the observations of everyday life. Due to its complexity, the model was simplified by integrating the effects of vertical and horizontal excitations, which revealed the possibility of two stable and two unstable steady-state solutions. In response to horizontal excitation, the system exhibits a Hopf bifurcation, resulting in an oscillatory-translation movement near the pivot, causing coffee spillage. A particular movement pattern, resembling a star shape, was also observed and explained. The study's findings provide a potential answer to the frequently asked question, 'Why do we lose coffee when running?' The answer lies in the transition of the system from a steady-state with minimal oscillations to a spilling state characterized by larger oscillations. The critical factor here is not the amplitude but the frequency of these oscillations. When this model's results are compared with another study on loss of cargo, it becomes evident that the spilling phenomenon is rooted in a deeper mathematical structure. The work presented here bridges the gap between theoretical and experimental research, resolving a long-standing puzzle and highlighting the connection between carrying liquids and falling over. In conclusion, the developed model facilitates the exploration of stability and movement patterns in coupled excitable and oscillatory systems, enabling the identification of steady-state solutions, their stability, and the conditions necessary for potential applications in bio-inspired technologies. Furthermore, we examine the equivalence of this condition with other, related operators being C-normal. Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional (such as skewing) transformations, then we outline general robustness validation strategies for all categories. Additionally, we design unique validation protocols tailored to a variety of specific transformation scenarios. Experimental results on multiple frequent three-dimensional transformations demonstrate the exceptional performance of TPC surpassing current standards with notable improvements. As an example, our method achieves significant enhancement in validated accuracy when dealing with twisting transformation along the z-axis (within a 20-degree range) from 20.3% to 83.8%. All code and models are available for use at https://github.com/Qianhewu/Point-Cloud-Smoothing. Emails for questions or discussions are available upon request. Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for
inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information.
Building upon successful applications of tensor decomposition in static graph
completions, we introduce Time-LowFER - an extension of the low-rank factorization
model that is both efficient in parameters and attentive to time constraints.
We recognize current time representation approaches' shortcomings and suggest a
cycle-aware time-encoding framework for time characteristics that is universally
applicable and provides a more comprehensive time representation. Our unified
framework focuses on processing time-sensitive data within temporal knowledge graph
embeddings. Experimental results show that our proposed solutions equal or outperform
state-of-the-art models using semantic matching on multiple evaluation metrics. The
source code for our method is available at https://github.com/jbarnesspain/TDFER. Our
approach has been tested on datasets such as Yelp, Google Events, and EventCal.

In the field of rigid-body impact sound synthesis, the sound produced by the ground is often overlooked. However, in this study, an idealized ground sound model, rooted in elastodynamic theory, is used to determine under which conditions ground sound is perceivable, rather than being masked by the sound produced by the impacting object or its transient vibrations. An analytical model derived from this theory allows for the calculation of the acceleration of the ground surface in a precise and mathematically closed form, which can then be applied in various simulation methods to generate the sound waves. It is found that ground sound can be audible under certain circumstances when the sound produced by the impacting object is inaudible, specifically, it can be louder than the sound produced by the object's transient vibrations in certain frequency ranges. Furthermore, it has been found that ground sound can be audible over long distances and that its frequency range can extend far beyond the audible range of the object's transient vibrations. Ultimately, it is demonstrated that ground sound can provide a direct and unobscurred audio representation of an impact. A prevalent form of Bell nonlocality known as "perfect Bell nonlocality" has been extensively studied. It has been previously considered exclusive to specific scenarios involving zero-error correlations from qubit/pqubit systems. However, this paper showcases a perfect demonstration of Bell nonlocality from non-zero error rates specifically in pqubit systems. Unlike traditional inequality-based demonstrations, this paper relies on a different concept involving zero-error communications. It is demonstrated that any perfect Bell experiment with three or more parties in pqubit systems can be replicated using a protocol involving zero-error communications among non-adjacent parties in a graph, without yielding any new inequalities through graph representations. This graph representation in question is inherently difficult to satisfy in any local real-world scenario, thereby serving as a perfect Bell nonlocality demonstration. It is also established that this graph representation is equivalent to an older concept known as "Bell inequalities in d dimensions" when considering the specific case of three-party pqubit systems. Lastly, this paper does justice to the original study by Lemerli et al., who first explored this concept in three-party pqubit systems, although this paper does not claim to build upon their work directly. It does, however, offer a more comprehensive approach to understanding and satisfying the Bell inequalities in question. A newly created hydrogen boride monolayer, existing in the Cmmm phase, exhibits potential as a superconductor due to similarities with MgB2 and an abundance of hydrogen within its structure. Utilizing density functional theory, we've used first-principles calculations to investigate its electronic, vibrational, and superconducting properties. Contrary to expectations, however, the hydrogen boride system fails to possess a notable superconducting critical temperature. Hydrogen in this compound impairs the bonding between boron atoms, thereby reducing the effectiveness of electron-phonon interaction. Further analysis into potential improvements reveals that doping this system with electrons or holes yields unsatisfactory results. Ultimately, the critical temperature's limitations stem from the vanishing hydrogen influence on the Fermi level states, predominantly controlled by boron's p states. Consequently, substantial amounts of hydrogen-like states near the Fermi level are essential for attaining significant superconducting critical temperatures in such hydrogenated monolayers. The methods and findings from this research may be applied to various other hydrogenated compounds, enabling the optimization of their superconducting properties. The calculated results indicate that an electron or hole doping of n = 1/d, with d representing the interatomic spacing, triggers a noticeable drop in the binding energy of the dimer phonons. Although this reaction is reminiscent of MgB2's response to doping, the superconducting output remains unresponsive to these stimuli, having failed to reach critical temperatures exceeding 5 K. Doping does nonetheless lead to an increase in the electron-phonon coupling's intensity, with the Foley-Martin ratio ranging from 2.05 to 2.85 for the doped hydrogen boride. The Foley-Martin ratio's variation is largely attributed to the doping-induced displacement of the hydrogen atom. Moreover, this shift triggers an increase in the phonon's energy and causes the 2f-like states to rise above the Fermi level. The calculated results from our study contradict the assumption that hydrogen within these monolayers would necessarily boost their superconducting critical temperatures. Rather, the hydrogen's impact is more complex, primarily influencing the electronic structures rather than the Fermi level states directly. Consequently, the critical temperatures of these hydrogenated monolayers are likely to remain subthreshold for superconductivity throughout the year 2023. The methods and findings from this research may be applied to various other hydrogenated compounds, enabling the optimization of their superconducting properties. To safeguard against electric and electronic failures, a backup system is triggered by an arbitration logic that prioritizes functional safety above all else. To uphold the standards set forth by ISO 26262, rigorous testing of this logic is mandatory. Through this validation, one can confidently ensure the reliability of system responses in times of crisis and prevent aberrant system states from materializing. Traditional safety assessment tools are often inadequate in this capacity, prompting us to propose an advanced method centered around formal verification, leveraging model checking in particular. To demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, we carefully recreate the driving system's dynamics, define and formalize key safety criteria, and scope the analysis within the guidelines specified by ISO 26262. Upon successfully verifying a high-automation fail-safe logic aligned with industrial standards, we discovered critical errors previously unaccounted for in more conventional evaluations, thereby significantly enhancing the reliability of automotive safety-critical systems. To the best of our knowledge, this verification method represents the most comprehensive evaluation of a driving system fail-safe logic to date. Our proposed technique, embodying a novel application of formal verification, has been fully integrated into an open-source model checking toolset available for public use and tailored specifically to address the distinctive needs of automated driving systems. This unique toolset showcases the full scope of our approach and serves as evidence of the feasibility and benefits associated with the application of formal verification in the domain of automotive safety-critical systems. Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is introduced that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence and utilizes the Koopman operator to handle nonlinear relationships, thus extending the approach to a broad spectrum of applications. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through clustering of a linear system, the non-linear 39-bus transmission network, and variables derived from atmospheric data in the Amazon rainforest. Furthermore, this paper highlights the integration of this operator into the analysis of temporal data, enabling the development of a comprehensive framework that facilitates community detection, enabling the derivation of dynamic state models and effective monitoring of anomalies. Experimental findings demonstrate the method's capabilities and showcase its performance compared to established clustering algorithms. The researchers make the code and atmospheric data set publicly available for further study. Recent research into Leibnizian calculus has centered on evaluating different fundamental approaches to describe its mathematical processes.  Many scholars, such as Ishiguro and Levey, rely on a Weierstrassian perspective; in contrast, Arthur draws comparisons to the Lawvere-Kock-Bell framework, a non-Archimedean approach known as Smooth Infinitesimal Analysis (SIA). A critical examination of Arthur's comparison reveals significant misunderstandings regarding the nature of the continuous, polygons with an infinite number of sides, and infinitesimal quantities. Additionally, claims by Rabouin and Arthur, suggesting that Leibniz considered infinite quantities to be inherently contradictory, rely on an incorrect blending of Leibnizian concepts of bounded and unbounded infinites - a distinction previously noted by early Knobloch. Instead, a framework developed by Robinson may provide a more accurate account of Leibnizian calculus, which can be formalized using a conservative axiomatic system for infinitesimal analysis called SPOT. This formalisation covers a broad range of concepts, including the behaviour of quantities, quantities with states, and magnitudes, as well as a generalisation of the concept of a bounded infinitesimal. This formalisation avoids the paradoxes of SIA and aligns more closely with the processes and concepts underlying Leibnizian calculus. Furthermore, a second formalisation is proposed in Deng, based on a generalisation of metric spaces, which also captures many of the key concepts of Leibnizian calculus. A comparison between these two frameworks highlights the similarities and differences between them, raising questions about which features are essential to Leibnizian calculus and which are not. In particular, the distinction between these two frameworks may provide insight into the celebrated controversy over who discovered calculus, Potter noting that the various interpretations of Leibnizian calculus are 'all equally valid'. Therefore, Robinson's framework of SPOT is preferred as it allows a formalisation that is both conservative and accurate. This research paper explores solving polynomial linear systems in the presence of errors using an evaluation-interpolation technique, with a focus on minimizing the number of computations required to recover the solution. This is crucial for solving systems in high dimensions, where processing efficiency is essential. Two key factors that affect the overall process are the number of points at which evaluations are conducted and the method used for interpolating the polynomial coefficients. This study introduces new bounds on the error tolerance for each point during the evaluation phase, which can be calculated more efficiently than existing limits. Furthermore, this work develops a dynamic interpolation process that allows for early termination based on an online error estimation technique. This approach leads to significant reductions in the computational cost, particularly in multi-variable polynomial systems. Two applications are provided to demonstrate the improved efficiency of this solution over existing ones. These examples cover the Euclidean algorithm for matrix factorization and a method for computing the affine hull of a set of points in $n$-dimensional space. Both of these problems can be cast as polynomial linear systems with specific properties. This research presents new and competitive bounds on the breakdown probabilities for both problems. This work is self-contained and may serve as a comprehensive introduction to solving polynomial linear systems with errors, in addition to offering improved solutions to the specific problems considered. A unified analytical equation of state for the equilibrium gas phase of pure alkali metals has been derived. This concise equation encompasses the perfect gas model, is applicable to all alkali metals, and accurately predicts their behavior across a broad pressure range (up to $\sim 10^5$~Pa) and temperature range (up to $\sim 3 \cdot 10^3$~K). Based on this equation of state, key thermodynamic properties such as internal energy, specific heat, isothermal compressibility, thermal expansion coefficient, and surface tension have been expressed in terms of measurable temperature and pressure. These properties are calculated with high precision, and in many cases, to an error margin of less than $0.5\%$. Furthermore, a generalized model for the van der Waals interaction energy between two sodium atoms has been introduced, which enables the simulation of cryogenic sodium under pressure. This model facilitates the prediction of sodium's liquid-vapor coexistence curve at temperatures below $173$~K. Additionally, a theoretical model for the critical point of alkali metals has been developed, and the resulting values for critical temperature, pressure, and density are in line with experimental data. These findings demonstrate that many thermodynamic properties of alkali metals can be accurately described using a simple, unified analytical model in conjunction with existing quantum chemical data. This model can be expanded to account for molecular species by incorporating intermolecular potentials. Consequently, this analytical model holds great potential for applications in both basic scientific research and diverse technological contexts. As such, the article concludes by outlining numerous possible areas of application. The required mathematical evidence is provided in an additional file appended to this article. In the context of vector-meson dominance model, properties of light vector mesons in local parity breaking mediums with chiral imbalance are explored. By utilizing a finite lowest-order local effective Lagrangian derived from QED for vector ρ and ω mesons, a mass spectrum as a function of momentum and chiral chemical potential is determined. Furthermore, in addition to the existing Chern-Simons effect, which differentiates the transverse polarizations of these mesons, a significant radiatively induced contribution arises at a few hundred MeV for momentum and chiral chemical potential. Importantly, the Lagrangian parameters' independence is confirmed, along with the outcome's consistency with the Gell-Mann, Levy, and Nambu models. Lastly, in the limit of zero chiral chemical potential, the outcomes converge with existing approaches. A brief discussion on the implications of these findings for heavy nuclear collisions is also presented. Based on this study's results, it is hypothesized that the vector-like Higgs in the Standard Model may induce a significant chiral imbalance in the environment of a heavy nucleus. Such a phenomenon could potentially manifest in the formation of parallel and perpendicular polarized ω-meson complexes and be detectable via the parallel and perpendicular polarization of electrons and muons. Furthermore, it is suggested that this mechanism could serve as a primary contributor to the chiral imbalance in heavy ion collisions. The possibility of detecting this effect in e+e- collisions at B-factory energies, along with future collisions at LHC and RHIC, is explored. It is estimated that the resulting electron and muon polarizations could be measurable in TESLA-type colliders with a 10^-3 order of magnitude deviation from the standard model predictions. The potential outcomes of these experiments on our understanding of the underlying quantum chromodynamics dynamics are also considered. It is conjectured that the resulting data could significantly enhance our comprehension of the QCD dynamics in the moderate to high temperature and chiral density region. The corollary that the generation of chiral imbalance in the environment of a heavy nucleus may be a generic feature of any phase of matter that is not completely symmetric is also explored. This concept could significantly affect the current understanding of nuclear matter and may require a reevaluation of the QCD at very low temperatures and densities. It is also proposed that the generated chiral imbalance could serve as a natural source of axial magnetic fields in heavy nuclei and may have significant implications for the study of neutron stars and the heavy ion collisions at the LHC. We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. In numerical simulations involving fluid dynamics, the Raviart-Thomas elements are widely used to approximate vector-valued variables like velocity or momentum. Nevertheless, the standard finite element methods that employ the lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas elements tend to have low spatial accuracy in the vector transport equation. This paper explores two methods that elevate the accuracy of transporting such vector-valued fields across curved surfaces in two-dimensional environments. One method enhances the transported field by projecting it onto a higher-order function space before solving the transport equation. In contrast, the other method utilizes a mixed finite element approach to concurrently solve for both the transported field and its vorticity, introducing a stabilisation strategy via a Streamline Upwind Petrov-Galerkin method. These schemes are validated and their performance compared in a series of numerical experiments involving both specially designed and standard rotating shallow-water models. Our findings indicate that the hybrid approach outperforms the projection method in achieving accurate transport results, and that the lowest-order Raviart-Thomas model remains a robust choice for solving the transport equation. Furthermore, the rotating shallow-water model appears to be a suitable substitute for the more complex fluid dynamics equation. Ultimately, the most accurate and robust strategy was identified as the combination of the rotating shallow-water model and the Streamline Upwind Petrov-Galerkin method. Our work is the first to initiate a study on discretising the vector transport equation using the lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas elements. As such, this research lays the groundwork for potential future applications and adaptations of the presented methods in the field of fluid dynamics. Additionally, the accompanying code is freely accessible on the Git repository: https://github.com/epfl-sharp-h2o/TransportRTQ1D.git. This ensures that the code remains self-descriptive and easily understandable by other researchers. To address these problems, experts employ fairness metrics, decentralized machine learning methods known as federated learning, or differential privacy. A pioneering approach, this study creates a unified ethical federated learning framework, seamlessly integrating all three techniques in harmony. The integration of differential privacy comes with an improved interpretation of the Privacy General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The study's source code is freely accessible. We have developed a numerical approach to maximize coupling efficiency in single-photon sources consisting of a quantum dot-cavity and a ridge waveguide by conducting simulations using the finite element method. A design optimized for a 1D nanobeam cavity yielded a notable source efficiency of 97.7 percent and an impressive Purcell factor of 38.6 for an isotropic dipole, primarily due to a combination of high index contrast between GaAs and SiO$_2$ materials and an effective cavity design that facilitated interference and minimized losses. However, we also identified mode mismatch as a limitation of our platform and devised an optimization technique to achieve high efficiency in single-photon sources. This method incorporates a taper section to smoothly bridge the mode mismatch between the cavity and the nanobeam, ultimately enhancing the Purcell factor and source efficiency. Furthermore, we observed the resilience of our design in the face of real-world fabrication imperfections affecting hole variation in the taper-nanobeam system. Our optimized design also facilitated single-cycle extraction of Purcell-enhanced emission from a two-level system and enabled the observation of Purcell-enhanced emission from a real-level diamond cavity. Additionally, we combined our optimized nanobeam design with a diamond cavity for a real-level diamond cavity. This led to enhanced Purcell-enhanced emission in the real-level diamond cavity. Our work contributes to the development of efficient on-chip single-photon sources, enabling applications in quantum computing and communication. In random systems, the scattering matrix correlates incident wave patterns with internal distributions within a volume, and previously this correlation was leveraged to increase energy delivered to a target. This study determines a general set of constraints and formulas governing the eigenvalues and modes within any given scattering setup - including complex geometries, and broad categories such as slabs and narrow channels. Our mathematical framework reveals limitations and correlations for intensity within system boundaries, and derived relationships provide a path towards optimizing delivery to specific areas within a scattering environment. Our findings demonstrate potential ways to realize high-efficiency, target-selective delivery in complex environments. In addition, our work in developing and applying a mathematical framework may contribute to understanding the spectral properties of generalized eigenvalues in other contexts. A microstrip-fed patch antenna designed to operate at mm-waves with broad bandwidth and a wide angle of coverage has been successfully created and tested for integration in planar arrays. The designed antenna has a significant bandwidth of 13.1%, operating between 34.1 GHz and 38.9 GHz, facilitated by the combination of a slotted microstrip patch with multiple resonances and an optimized microstrip matching circuit. Constructed using the low-cost RO3003 substrate with top and ground layers, this design accommodates simple integration with other microstrip and frontend components via top-layer microstrip coupling gap feed. The achieved wide beamwidth of 100-125 degrees is primarily due to strategically designed parasitic patches for the primary resonant frequency and inherently wide beamwidth for the second resonant frequency within the specified bandwidth, making this a highly efficient microstrip patch antenna for operation over a ground plane. The input impedance and radiation pattern observed through measured data closely agree with the simulated results. This design offers a practical solution for a highly efficient, wide-range, and broad-bandwidth mm-wave antenna suitable for array integration in various applications, particularly in wireless communication where wide beamwidth is beneficial for increasing coverage and efficiency. In contrast, broad-bandwidth alone often results in a depressed input impedance and decreased efficiency, while wide beamwidth alone causes a decline in gain and efficiency in array applications, as demonstrated by the observed trends in the simulated and measured data. This design successfully overcomes these limitations, showcasing its potential for highly efficient operation over a wide angle and broad bandwidth in mm-wave applications. Key performance metrics for this design include a wide beamwidth of 100-125 degrees, a broad bandwidth of 4.8 GHz (13.1% relative bandwidth) centered at approximately 36 GHz with two distinct resonant frequencies, and a low cross-polarization level of less than 10 dB over the specified bandwidth, as measured and consistent with the simulated data. The simple and versatile design utilizing the low-cost substrate with top and ground layers, combined with microstrip coupling feed and an optimized microstrip matching circuit for broad bandwidth and a wide angle of coverage, has been successfully implemented and experimentally validated for integration in planar arrays at mm-waves. This research will facilitate the creation of highly efficient, wide-range, and broad-bandwidth mm-wave microstrip patch antennas for various single-element and array applications in communication and other fields where wide beamwidth and broad bandwidth are beneficial. Using deepQ learning as an example, we successfully created rapid surface code decoders capable of handling multiple types of noise models. Moreover, the deepQ learning decoders can adapt to changing noise models and accurately recover the original quantum state even when part of the measurement data is faulty. The PHENIX Collaboration has collected data on direct photon-hadron correlations in 200 GeV/A Au$+$Au, $d$$+$Au, and $p$$+$$p$ collisions from 2006 to 2011. These findings reveal that cold nuclear matter has negligible effects on $d$$+$Au collisions. A notable disparity exists in hadron production between Au$+$Au and $p$$+$$p$ collisions. Hadrons with high momentum fractions are suppressed in Au$+$Au, whereas those with lower momentum fractions show increased yields, exceeding $p$$+$$p$ collisions. This excess, observed at large angles and low hadron $p_T$, is more pronounced for hadrons linked to lower-momentum direct photons, indicating an increased response of the medium to deposited energy. These hadrons' high-yield excess is consistent with a general collective effect, whose significance diminishes with increasing hadron $p_T$. This excess is 25% of the hadron's total yield for those hadrons within a given $p_T$ range and associated with 1-2 GeV direct photons. These findings are analogous to those from 2.76 TeV/Pb$+$Pb collisions. They imply that the medium responds to incoming high-energy partons by collectively producing a large number of off-momentum hadrons. Furthermore, the experimental data are compared to the VNI transport model, which successfully recreates the observed effects, including the production of medium-induced hadrons. Although the model provides a coherent explanation for these phenomena, it fails to account for the observed hadron production at forward angles. This discrepancy might be attributed to the model's inability to account for parton losses in the far forward region or the influence of anomalous J/$\psi$ yields. Additionally, the model's failure to accurately model direct photon yields in Au$+$Au collisions at energies > 20 GeV might be another contributing factor. Consequently, the model necessitates refinement, particularly regarding parton scattering in the far forward region, incorporating an alternative explanation for the observed hadron production at forward angles or incorporating radiative decays of open charm. Therefore, the direct photon-hadron correlations in Au$+$Au and $d$$+$Au collisions offer a profound understanding of the medium's response to high-energy partons, revealing a collective effect and a phenomenon that could be captured by the VNI transport model. A common issue in machine learning lies in striking a balance between optimizing performance and robustly handling out-of-distribution (OoD) scenarios. It combines the difference between two separate Cox-Ingersoll-Ross processes, incorporating the deterministic-shift adjustment. For quick alignment with the current swaption prices, the Gram-Charlier expansion is employed to calculate swaption prices within the proposed framework. Multiple numerical evaluations are performed, utilizing Monte-Carlo simulations, to showcase the benefits of this model, as evidenced by its similarity to the Hull-White one-factor model's Bermudan swaption prices on Bloomberg, and by its alignment with Bloomberg's constant maturity swap rates. Furthermore, the analysis reveals a strong correlation between the proposed model's basis spread and the Bloomberg-reference basis spread. Finally, the researchers simulate a plausible path for the model's volatility parameter, and demonstrate the model's ability to maintain long-term stability, as well as its ability to reproduce the observed yield curve volatility. Overall, the proposed model is shown to be highly effective in reproducing the observed yield curve, and is capable of accurately pricing Bermudan swaptions, thus making it a suitable candidate for practical use in the capital markets. Meta-analyses that include multiple trials based on shared study participants often report correlated effect sizes.  In such scenarios, employing cluster-robust variance estimators can effectively synthesize dependent effects, however these may produce inflated Type 1 errors in cases of a limited number of studies.  In order to improve the performance of robust estimators when dealing with small sample sizes, two new cluster-robust estimators have been developed.  Both estimators work by adjusting the estimated residual variances using only the diagonal entries of the hat matrix, resulting in asymptotic equivalence to previously proposed estimators such as the bias reduced linearization method.  This new approach is demonstrated in a simulation study on real world data, with particular application in bivariate meta-regression though it may also be utilized more broadly.  The proposed estimators have been implemented in the R package called'metaSBugs'.  Additional information can be found on the website: www.metaSBugs.com.  In the case of a limited number of studies, both variants may produce one- and two-tailed p-values that are overly conservative, though these may become less conservative as the number of studies increases.  This conservative characteristic could lead to spurious rejections in cases of a low number of studies where both the effect size and the study-specific residual variance are considered.  Consequently, p-values derived from these estimators may be deemed too conservative and could be addressed by incorporating additional data through a meta-analysis fusion technique called 'Bayesian fusion'.  This approach may also possess added benefits in terms of increased statistical power and improved estimation accuracy.  The proposed estimators have been evaluated in a series of simulations and applied in an analysis of 179 studies on cognitive functioning and their website is located at www.metaSBugs.com.  The site provides the necessary software for the analysis.  A notable case in point is the data on the link between smoking during pregnancy and infant weight that was collected from 132 studies.  The data was then examined using three different approaches:  first using ordinary robust estimators;  second using bias reduced linearization;  and third using the new approach implemented in the metaSBugs package.  The results from these analyses indicate that the new approach produces smaller estimates of bias and maintained asymptotic conservative properties when estimating a null hypothesis that there is no effect. High-performance computing systems rely heavily on fault tolerance to prevent data loss and ensure system reliability. Recent advances in non-volatile memory have made it feasible to achieve this, as data in such memory is preserved even during crashes. Nevertheless, the volatility of system caches still poses a challenge, as they may drop cache contents during a system crash, potentially leading to data corruption. To address this issue, a new research area known as algorithmic crash consistency has emerged, which aims to guarantee data integrity and correctness after system crashes by revisiting and revising program execution pathways. This study aims to demonstrate the feasibility of implementing algorithmic crash consistency in modern high-performance computing systems by highlighting a practical approach based on hardware support. Our proposed solution leverages the capabilities of modern CPUs, which enable efficient memory access management through hardware-defined consistent memory regions. Our results indicate that this solution can be integrated into existing systems with minimal performance overhead, while significantly enhancing data integrity and system reliability. Our experimental findings demonstrate that the latency associated with managing algorithmic crash consistency is comparable to other contemporary techniques. Moreover, the intrinsic elegance of our solution allows it to be integrated into high-level programming languages with minimal complexity. Our results show that, in practice, the overhead of integrating this solution into C++ is acceptable and comparable to other approaches. Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. Wikipedia's full category page was used to determine the model's capabilities for producing comprehensive hierarchies. The results from our evaluations on three datasets, including two previously unseen Wikipedia categories and web pages from cohealth.com, demonstrate the superiority of HDTM over existing methods in both hierarchy production and readability. The corresponding code for replicating the results is available at https://github.com/jjjouimont/HDTM. In addition, the Wikipedia categories are available at https://github.com/jjjouimont/HDTM_Wiki_Categories. The generated hierarchies for Wikipedia and cohealth.com are available in HTML format at https://github.com/jjjouimont/HDTM_Wiki_Categories. HDTM's ability to meet scalability needs is attributed to its distributed processing model, which allows for efficient computation on large datasets by treating topics as real-time, continuously evolving components of the underlying information network. The model also employs more intuitive categories, eliminating the need for redundant and less relevant nodes, and includes an inherent level of hierarchy by ranking topics based on their occurrence across the dataset. The effectiveness of HDTM is confirmed by our evaluations, which found the model outperformed current methods in both hierarchy production and readability, and found the model's characteristics comparable to those of human-generated hierarchies. In particular, HDTM was preferred over Random and Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) in terms of readability, and was preferred to LDA in terms of hierarchy production. Additionally, HDTM was found to capture the underlying structure of the information network, and was found to have similar characteristics as human-generated hierarchies. As a compact star's density increases, sound velocity approaches the conformal limit at high densities, satisfying the causality limit while its detailed behavior remains disputed. It's hypothesized that dense matter sound velocity can be an indicator of a deconfinement phase transition, possibly exhibiting a distinctive relationship with density. Our work delves into the fundamental properties of dense matter sound velocity and the adiabatic index within neutron stars, quark stars, and hybrid stars.  By simulating the hadron-quark phase transition with different interface tension, we found the sound velocity's expected behavior could also arise from the quark phase's nonperturbative properties. Compounds composed of potassium ($A=$ K, Rb, Cs) combined with boron in a 2:1 ratio, exhibit unique cubic structures called the Laves phase with a specific Fd$\bar{3}$m symmetry. The arrangement of atoms within these crystals permits the existence of chirally behaving phonons, which correspond to atoms circling their equilibrium positions. Given that inversion symmetry and time reversal symmetry govern the total pseudo-angular momentum of the system, this momentum is zero. By introducing dopants, researchers find this condition is breached, resulting in a new crystal structure - tetragonal ($P$4$\bar{3}$m) - and subsequently a non-zero total pseudo-angular momentum. Ultimately, this property has significant implications for the magnetic properties of these doped materials.

Three-dimensional topological insulators can be identified by a magnetoelectric coefficient with a quantized value, but it lacks observable manifestations when time-reversal symmetry prevails due to opposing influences of internal and external states cancelling out. The distinctive response characteristic of a topological insulator manifests as a nonlinear magnetoelectric effect, whose field-theoretical properties and computational models are explored. This contrasts with another phenomenon where a magnetoelectric interaction traps a charge equal to $\pm e/2$ upon exposure to a magnetic monopole, commonly referred to as the Witten effect. The time-reversal symmetry being explicitly violated, as in the case of a Zeeman field influencing the surface electrons, can allow a description of a topological insulator's electromagnetic response via the surface electrons undergoing a half-integer quantum Hall effect. As a result, key signals from experiments designed to measure a topological insulator's magnetoelectric coefficient may arise from observations of edge states undergoing a half-integer quantum Hall effect instead. The time-reversal symmetry being broken gives rise to various phenomena such as the appearance of gaps in momentum space that are localised to one edge of the surface, an effect that can be seen in both numerical simulations and experimental data on bi-layer graphene and multi-layer graphene, which exhibit a Hall effect characteristic of a topological insulator. The time-reversal symmetry being violated leads to edge localised states that exhibit counter-propagating characteristics, an effect that can be observed in experiments involving electric field measurements on notches cut into samples of a topological insulator made from MoS2. The Witten effect, an effect that occurs when a charge is trapped by a magnetic monopole, is shown not to occur in three-dimensional topological insulators when time-reversal symmetry is violated, but it is argued that it does occur when the time-reversal symmetry is broken. For the first time, we establish a link between Arnold tongue patterns in parameter space and the diffusive behavior of delay systems. Contrary to expectation, this increase in diffusion is accompanied by a considerable decrease in the system's effective dimensionality. Additionally, we identify novel interwound attractors, known as Rossler spirals, in the Arnol'd finger regimes, as well as a distinct family of quasi-periodic routes exhibiting scaling properties. These routes, unlike those observed in traditional chaotic diffusion, exhibit scaling exponents independent of the system's overall dimensionality. Lastly, we explore the possibility of experimentally observing chaotic diffusion in delay systems, taking advantage of the stabilization of diffusive coherence in the latter. This could potentially facilitate the development of novel, delay-based chaos engines with novel features. In particular, it is suggested that Arnold finger regimes, with their distinctive quasi-periodic scaling, could be realized through geospatial distributions of time delay in networks of coupled oscillators. Additionally, the idea of utilizing Arnold's method to achieve chaotic diffusion in high-dimensional delay systems via quasi-periodic scalings, and the possibility of realizing quasi-periodic scalings in biological and other living systems, are also discussed. In conclusion, we examine the extensive array of novel attractors, ranging from planar trimodes to quasi-periodic scalings, that can be achieved by means of Arnold's method for modulated delay systems. These are discovered to be distinct from all other types of delay systems, while simultaneously providing numerous new avenues for the theoretical and experimental exploration of delay nonlinear dynamics. Ultimately, it is contended that quasi-periodic scalings, with their extensive distribution across parameter space, are inherently associated with the extensive, diffusive coherence observed in modulated delay systems. We provide rigorous definitions for sound and sufficient denotational and operational interpretations of the stochastic lambda calculus. By establishing a strong connection between these interpretations, we demonstrate their equivalence. Furthermore, we introduce a general framework for constructing stochastic universal domains and prove that any stochastic lambda calculus with a sound operational semantics can be translated to a domain-based semantics. This framework is expected to contribute to the broader field of stochastic domain theory. We also explore methods for defining higher-order probability distributions and investigate the relationship between notions of approximate equality for stochastic values, proposing a method for comparing these equalities based on trace semantics. Ultimately, we demonstrate that the notions of operational and denotational semantics are equally effective in guiding the definition of a stochastic lambda calculus for a specific domain family. We further reveal the connections between these interpretations and ideas from quantum programming. Specifically, we define a relational interpretation of the quantum lambda calculus and establish a correspondence between its denotational and operational formulations. Discussions among developers encompass a variety of interactions, including in-person conversations and online comments, which are beneficial to label as relevant to software design for documentation and improvement purposes. This is made possible through a process known as design mining. Two essential characteristics of design mining are prevalent in current methods: the reliance on multiple participants for discussion mining and the application of conventional information retrieval or neural techniques, often incorporating features such as word embeddings. This is surprising, given that human convergence, or the consistency of labeled mining conclusions, might be expected to occur naturally without complex techniques. In this study, we examine human convergence on software design discussions by leveraging a diverse set of annotated discussions and demonstrate that conventional IR methods may not be necessary for stable design mining conclusions when multiple participants' opinions are combined. Our proposed approach, Simplified Design Mining, is built around a basic word frequency-based similarity metric and is particularly useful for large-scale discussion threads, such as those found on GitHub. In our experiments, SDM produced mining conclusions comparable to those of more sophisticated methods, such as neural-based approaches, thus validating its effectiveness. Moreover, SDM's reliance on basic features renders it highly scalable, enabling it to handle discussions to the order of tens of thousands of messages. In contrast to existing design mining methods, SDM thus represents a more practical and efficient solution. Ultimately, our work implies that design mining conclusions may be reached more easily and consistently than previously thought, provided that a sufficient number of participants' opinions are properly aggregated. This has promising broader potential, extending to other technical topic mining applications. Proximal methods can efficiently uncover the underlying pattern in nonsmooth optimization problems, and, in many cases, identifying this structure is a free byproduct, also enhancing the convergence rate once aligned with that of the problem's optimal solution. Nonetheless, pinpointing the exact structure is not possible without adaptation. By assuming a proximal gradient method is able to recognize the differentiability manifolds in a nonsmooth objective, we show that incorporating Riemannian Newton-like techniques specifically designed for these manifolds can result in a significantly improved convergence rate. Moreover, our theoretical findings are substantiated by experimental results in various test problems. It is worth noting that, much like how the proximal gradient method benefits from (often unintended) structure recognition, our algorithm takes advantage of this recognition to aid the proximal gradient method. This interaction is beneficial for all, including when the proximal gradient method would converge at a rate of O(1/k) iterations. Additionally, when the proximal gradient method is able to converge at a rate of O(log(k)/k) iterations, our algorithm achieves a converged solution in O(log(k)/k) iterations. Additionally, when the proximal gradient method converges at a rate of O(k/badk) iterations, our algorithm achieves a converged solution in O(k/badk) iterations. In all cases, the number of Newton steps required to refine the proximal gradient solution is bounded by O(log(k)/k) or O(k/badk). Based on this, we propose an algorithm that iteratively performs a proximal gradient step, followed by a Newton step using Riemannian optimization techniques, and this algorithm is evaluated against current state-of-the-art methods in nonsmooth optimization, including SDP-BOGD and Choco. Our algorithm outperforms these methods in a range of test problems, including matrix factorization, rank minimization, and data fusion, often by substantial margins. Ultimately, our algorithm represents a novel, fast, and robust solution to nonsmooth optimization, and this solution is made possible by the proximal gradient method's ability to identify the differentiability manifolds in the problem. Due to the nonsmooth nature of the problem, we are unable to visualize the structure, but theoretical and experimental results validate the algorithm's fast convergence rate. The source code for our algorithm is publicly available at https://github.com/sameersayed/Newton-on-Manifolds. This research was funded by ANR-19-CE47A-0006.

Our team employed photonic technology to revolutionize the conventional method of spectroscopy, enabling on-device spectral cross-correlation using a template. This was achieved by designing photonic devices with intricately modulated transmission spectra, thus making full-scale spectrographic cameras capable of cross-correlation without the need for dispersion. By incorporating these devices, our design allows for the inclusion of up to 300 imaging elements within a single photonic device, thus amplifying the detection capability of exotic celestial objects. Furthermore, our design's miniature size facilitates the miniaturization of telescopes, thus paving the way for the development of compact, miniature telescopes capable of detecting rare celestial entities. Finally, our research incorporated the diffusion process of light to explore the performance limits of these photonic devices, especially at low light levels, thus enabling the detection of distant or exotic celestial objects. Ultimately, our research mapped the spatial distribution of light to explore its potential in exploring the binary evolution of stellar systems. This was done by designing a 4-inch photonic device with  122 individual elements and transmitting it onto a microfiber, thus exhibiting potential in various photonic applications, particularly in spectroscopy. Additionally, our research demonstrated the transmission of over 90% of light in the 400-900 nm spectral range with resolution variations of 0.078-0.630 angstroms and transmitting phases of up to 2pi, thus exhibiting the capabilities of our photonic devices in spectroscopic applications. Finally, our research reached a depth limit of around 25th magnitude in a single 4-inch photonic device with  122 elements and a 0.6 Angstrom resolution, thus showcasing the capabilities of these photonic devices in various astronomical applications. Imitation learning seeks to bypass the complexity of creating optimal reward functions for agent training by utilizing expert behavior instead. The challenge lies in environments that are modeled as Markov Decision Processes, and current imitation algorithms often rely on access to expert demonstrations within the exact same environment in which the imitation policy is to be learned. When discrepancies arise between expert and agent domains due to varying dynamics, perspectives, or morphologies, imitation tasks become infeasible for straight-forward application. This paper proposes a new framework that establishes correspondences across disparate domains using only unaligned trajectories containing states from the expert's viewpoint. The framework leverages cycle-consistency constraints in both the state space and the action space to solve the imitation problem. The efficacy of this approach is validated through experiments on diverse robot domains. Specifically, the focus lies on robotic manipulation in the Real World Robot Challenge and a setup comprising a robotic arm manipulating objects in both simulated and real worlds. Those experiments show that the proposed method successfully bridges the domain gap in the state space while accurately mapping actions to their corresponding counterparts, thus demonstrating improved performance in both direct and indirect settings. Those results imply that actions taken by an expert in another domain can be mimicked through the introduction of the proposed cycle-consistency constraint. A major uncertainty in determining the initial mass function of the first (Population III) stars hinges on the ultimate fate of secondary protostars that form in the accretion disk - whether they will merge or remain separate. We concentrate on this issue and propose a mechanism, similar to that which was previously proposed by [Kitakoshi et al. 2018], to explain the initial star formation in the Early Universe. We simulate magnetohydrodynamic simulations of disk fragmentation surrounding a Population III protostar and demonstrate that when the initial amplification of the magnetic field is increased from $10^{-6}$ to $10^{-4}$ Gauss, the disk fragmentation is completely eliminated. However, under similar conditions but without magnetic field, the fragmentation remains unaltered. We explain the discrepancy in the magnetic field simulations of $10^{-6$ and $10^{-4}$ Gauss as a result of the differing Ohmic dissipation rates that affect the instability criterion in the accretion disk. As a result, the amplification of the magnetic field to $10^{-4}$ Gauss or higher in the accretion disk surrounding a Population III protostar could prevent the fragmentation and ensure that a single star forms. This finding offers a potential answer to the long-standing question of how a single star could have been formed in the Early Universe while also accounting for the formation of multiple metal-rich stars in the present Universe. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.  Therefore, providing convicted offenders with mandated mental health treatment as part of their sentence appears to decrease recidivism and has the potential to be cost-effective by decreasing future crime.  An efficient way to increase the effectiveness of the justice system and reduce future crime is to offer mental health treatment to convicted individuals.  This policy change could lead to considerable cost savings and improve public safety. Radio maps are being explored as a promising approach to equip advanced wireless networks with situational awareness. They will likely serve a pivotal function in enabling UAV communications by allowing the assessment of signal strength and interference levels at unknown locations. Different from conventional surveying methods, which depend on station-based measurements, radio maps are estimated using data collected from mobile entities called radiometers. The key challenge in generating these maps is separating the varying channels in the data collected by the radiometers as they move around. The main obstacle in accomplishing this is the observed cross-channel correlations caused by the movement of the radiometers themselves. In this paper, we introduce a novel algorithm inspired by past research in geolocation databases, which uses the data collected by the radiometers and their locations to estimate the positions of the transmitters. The proposed algorithm, referred to as Joint Estimation Uplink (JEUplink), uses a simplified model of the channel cross-talk and uses the data collected by the radiometers to estimate the positions of the transmitters. The effectiveness of the JEUplink algorithm is demonstrated in simulations using real-world data. The simulated results show that it can significantly improve radio map estimation even in the presence of cross-talk. Moreover, it can handle situations with a large number of channels. This paper outlines a novel approach, GLA, for identifying unusual patterns in discrete time series by leveraging Hidden Markov Models and clustering techniques. At its core lies the comparison of sequential data segments. The process involves first mapping these segments to suitable Hidden Markov Models via the Baum-Welch algorithm, followed by a simplification of the probability distributions associated with these models. The resulting representation is then analyzed through a clustering method or an outlier detection tool to pinpoint anomalies. Notably, the use of Hidden Markov Models could be replaced by alternative models, such as dynamic Bayesian networks, without affecting the overall method. The proposed algorithm operates in an unsupervised setting, eliminating the need for manual data labeling. The feasibility and performance of this method are demonstrated through its application to simulated and real-world data. The simulated data serve as a controlled environment to assess the efficacy of this technique, while its application to operational data includes analyzing the running patterns of late aircraft at Chicago's O'Hare Airport. The results indicate that HLAA is capable of accurately detecting anomalies in various contexts. This research delves into a multi-aspect approach to person verification incorporating auditory, visual, and thermal modalities. Given the efficacy of auditory and visual modality combination, this investigation extends to exploring the effect of incorporating thermal images on verification robustness. Specifically, state-of-the-art deep learning architectures were applied to establish unimodal, bimodal, and trimodal verification systems which were compared under optimal and impaired conditions. Moreover, a comparison of fusion methods using simple score aggregation and soft attention techniques was also conducted. Experimental results obtained on the SpeakingFaces dataset showed that a multi-aspect verification system outperforms unimodal and bimodal approaches by significant margins, both in noise-free and noise-present scenarios. To promote research in the area and guarantee replicability of this research, our source code, pre-trained models, and dataset preprocessed for analysis were made freely accessible on our GitHub repository. Additionally, this study investigates the distribution of deep features from respective modalities and their correlation using histogram equalization and heat maps. Finally, this study seeks to understand deep models through the analysis of their activation patterns via Backpropagation Through Time and Class Activation Maps. A multi-aspect approach was found to be more robust than unimodal and bimodal verification systems, and it exhibited increased resistance to noise. Importantly, this study underscores the value of examining person verification from multiple modalities and encourages researchers to explore multi-aspect verification as a potential replacement for traditional auditory and visual modality combinations.
