To study this highly interacting system, we developed a family of multi-band Hubbard models exhibiting exact pairing ground states across all symmetries. Through analytical computations, we discovered that many-body excitations are governed by an effective single-particle Hamiltonian based on the non-interacting wave functions of the system. Furthermore, we found a zero-energy excitation characteristic to these bound states with dispersion determined by the minimal quantum metric. Using the framework of topological quantum chemistry, we categorize the bound state spectrum, leading to the identification of Cooper pairs exhibiting Weyl nodes, high angular momentum pairing, and fragile topological features. Our analysis also demonstrates that electron kinetic energy as a perturbation maximizes pairing strength at half filling, similar to the phenomenon observed in twisted bilayer graphene. Lastly, we discuss the pairing symmetry of a specific, experimentally studied model based on a honeycomb lattice and explore the boundary between electron, hole, and half-filled regimes. Our theoretical conclusions indicate that electron-rich conditions are required to optimize pairing strength in such systems. Presence-absence data is represented as binary vectors or matrices consisting of zeros and ones, typically denoting the presence of something in a specific location. These data types commonly appear in research contexts such as ecological studies, genetic information, and linguistic analyses examining word occurrences in texts. Clustering methods can effectively apply to this data for a range of purposes including the identification of geographically linked species groups, known as biotic elements. Various clustering approaches can be utilized to process such data including the use of latent class mixtures under the assumption of local independence, hierarchical clustering based on the Jaccard distance, or applying continuous data methods to the multi-dimensional scaling representation of distances. These clustering methods vary conceptually and cannot easily be compared theoretically. To address this, we conduct an in-depth comparative analysis through simulation studies grounded in models for species distribution to evaluate their respective performances.

In our experiments, we analyzed the performance of various features in combination with BERT and examined the impact of using BERT on the identification of the offender. Our final submission showed consistency with our observed pre-submission performance in both tasks. Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in both engineering and medical fields for creating detailed images of internal structures within various subjects and objects. Since most X-ray sources emit X-rays of multiple energy levels, which vary in their absorption rates, the process of reconstructing images typically involves a reverse ray transformation process. Omitting these variations may result in distorted images, particularly when the object or subject contains contrasting materials. To address this issue, an alternative reconstruction approach, known as polyenergetic CT reconstruction, has been developed but it suffers from a common problem of noise. In this paper, we introduce a non-convex variational model that not only denoises and reconstructs images but also decomposes them into their constituent materials. To achieve this, we combine these tasks with a prior constraint, referred to as an anisotropic total variation of Wavlet domain. Through various numerical experiments, our model has shown significant noise reduction and reconstruction improvements over existing methods. Additionally, our results are both accurate and stable, even with artificially introduced noise at multiple energy levels. Our study offers a groundbreaking solution to the problem of CT image reconstruction, denoising and material separation. Interestingly, our model leads to a minimization problem that has an optimal solution, referred to as a optimal solution minimization (OSM). Due to its complexity, we resort to solving it iteratively and convergently, referred to as an iterative and convergent approach (ICA). Our study offers a novel and effective method for ICA. Furthermore, our model leads to a problem of variational total variation (VTV) and due to its non-convex nature, we resort to solving it through the use of a proximal algorithm and through several numerical experiments, our model has shown to be an effective method for VTV. Our study offers a novel and effective method for VTV. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that our model has the ability to resolve (or handle) penalized problems, referred to as PTV, and through several numerical experiments, our model has shown to be an effective method for PTV. Our study offers a novel and effective method for PTV. Finally, through several numerical experiments, our model has shown to be an effective method for CT, denoising and material decomposition (CMD) and it has the ability to handle (or resolve) CT, denoising and material decomposition (CDD) and CDM. Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with limited resources is a complex challenge, largely due to the scarcity of labeled data and limited language knowledge (dictionaries and language models). A specific obstacle is encountered in deciphering historical ciphers, which often employ fictional alphabets to conceal the contents. To overcome this problem, this study presents a novel approach to develop a straightforward method for creating composite datasets from unlabeled documents containing visual cues of written text. Additionally, it proposes a simplified yet effective dataset augmentation technique to enhance the performance of existing state-of-the-art models. Both methods are tested on the "Cifres" dataset, which comprises ciphertext written in the Catalan dialect, and on the widely used IAM dataset. The evaluation indicates that the proposed methods outperform the existing state-of-the-art models on the "Cifres" dataset. Furthermore, they display comparable or superior performance to those models trained with extensive supervised training on the widely used IAM dataset. Importantly, the techniques presented in this study are adaptable to various other datasets of handwritten text and can be applied even if a single fully written page is available. Leveraging unlabeled documents may seem paradoxical in the context of HTR, given that it typically relies heavily on supervised training, but this study demonstrates that the performance of existing models can be significantly enhanced by employing the methods presented, primarily through dataset augmentation. To validate the proposed methods, the performance of three state-of-the-art models was evaluated on three datasets: the "Cifres" dataset, the widely used IAM dataset, and the Rimes dataset. The evaluation indicates that the newly proposed methods outperform the existing models on the widely used IAM dataset and the Rimes dataset. We have developed a novel storage approach that significantly accelerates the convergence of large-scale diagonalization in ab initio nuclear structure calculations. This innovative method was successfully demonstrated in calculations for the calcium-42 and calcium-43 isotopes and isotones using the spectroscopic nuclei framework. Our calculations were conducted with a high level of precision, specifically with a maximum model space of 11 million Fock space basis states for calcium-42 and 17 million for calcium-43. This remarkable achievement marks a significant advancement in the field, allowing for detailed insight into the nuclear wave functions. Furthermore, we have achieved a new level of precision in the calculations of energy and spectroscopic factors, with an error margin of less than 10 kiloelectronvolts for energy and 5 percent for spectroscopic factors. This level of precision was previously unreachable for such medium-light nuclei through conventional storage methods. Our strategies for enhancing computational efficiency include exploiting symmetry, dividing up the model space, and utilizing the characteristics of low-lying states. This new approach enables calculations for larger-scale model spaces, thereby yielding more accurate ab initio nuclear structure results. Our findings for calcium-42 and calcium-43 include newly predicted energy and spectroscopic factor data for the gamma-ray decay modes of omega and Xi particles. Our calculations also demonstrated a high level of agreement with experimental data, with an error margin of less than 10 percent for energy and 10 percent for spectroscopic factors. Our research further highlights the significance of 40Ar as a critical nucleus in the study of regional nuclear structure and reveals the potential for a new decay mode in calcium-42. Moreover, our study on calcium isotopes offers valuable insights into the development and changes in nuclear structure across the calcium series. Our work in this research aligns with the recommendations set forth in the 2019 International Nuclear Structure and Decay Nuclear Physics Workshop. Ultimately, our innovative storage method has opened up new possibilities and paves the way for the in-depth study of heavy nuclei through precise ab initio calculations. High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL), and a do-all operation that is both parallel and efficient.  As a result, DynaSOAr offers improved memory usage, reduced fragmentation, and superior performance to leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by concurrently managing both memory allocation and memory access through atomic operations.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr's approach allows for significant speedup and memory management efficiency gains, as demonstrated by our benchmark results, which show that it outperforms other top GPU memory allocators by up to 3.3 times for geometric mean.  Our research further endorses the feasibility of object-oriented programming for SIMD devices, as well as the superiority of lock-free programming over traditional atomic operations.  To showcase the performance and efficiency of the DynaSOAr framework, we developed a suite of benchmarks, known as the SOA-Benchmark suite, which comprises 13 benchmarks inspired by real-world applications and characterized by SMMO paradigms.  Our research further reveals that a significant portion of these benchmarks can be successfully parallelized on GPUs using DynaSOAr, as evidenced by our benchmark results, which show that DynaSOAr achieves significant speedup and memory management efficiency gains over the current state-of-the-art approaches.  Our findings are crucial for developers, as they indicate that a substantial class of applications can be efficiently parallelized on GPUs using SMMO paradigms, which can be further accelerated using the DynaSOAr framework.  To facilitate easy adoption of this class of applications, we created a public and easily accessible DynaSOAr repository, as well as the SOA-Benchmark suite, which can be used by developers for evaluating the performance of new memory allocators and benchmarked applications. In various fields, ensuring decision functions maintain their optimal performance under changing conditions, even with limited knowledge of their environment, is a top priority. Our study introduces an approach for quantifying how well decision functions withstand uncertainty in the form of credal Bayesian networks, which are parametric models representing the unknown environment with confidence intervals on key variables. Focusing on the 'Maximum Marginal Probability' (MARmax) issue – the maximum possible error probability when misclassifying data, given varying parameter possibilities – our approach transforms MARmax into a more manageable problem on a probabilistic circuit with restrictions. Utilizing an efficient simplification, we provide a theoretically grounded upper limit to MARmax, calculated within linear time relative to the circuit's size, and our experiments demonstrate that this bound is usually precise, and our approach outperforms existing solutions in terms of efficiency. Additionally, our research highlights that MARmax assessment enables effective data depletion for boosting classification robustness, and our findings show that this method results in higher robustness levels when compared to standard approaches. Our code and data are accessible via an online repository. This research was presented at IJCAI 2021 and a revised version is being submitted for publication in a journal. In a supersolid Bose-Einstein condensate with a spin-orbit coupling, an accelerated impurity atom exhibits oscillations that mirror Bloch oscillations in solid matter, despite causing condensate excitements that give rise to internal phonon modes. However, these oscillations have no impact on the condensate's roton minimum position, thereby preserving its periodic matter wave pattern. Notably, the oscillations fade primarily due to wavepacket dispersal; yet, by assuming the impurity behaves as a bright soliton, the decay can be largely countered. Furthermore, this soliton scenario facilitates a theoretical description of a supersolid condensate using the Lee-Huang-Yang model. Ultimately, this new approach may enable the experimental observation of accelerated solitons within supersolid condensates. Suggestions for future research are also provided. In particular, we propose a feasible experimental protocol in Rb-87 to verify our theoretical predictions regarding the behavior of solitons within supersolid condensates. This proposed experiment could yield notable results within a timescale of tens of minutes. In addition to validating our theoretical model using phase-contrast microscopy, this experiment could also reveal unanticipated phenomena related to soliton formation and supersolid Bose-Einstein condensate interaction. These potential outcomes arise from the theoretical model's assumptions and simplified modeling of the spin-orbit coupling as a uniform external field. Consequently, this unexplored interaction may give rise to soliton patterns that deviate from perfect Gaussian shapes, thereby affecting the accelerates impurity atom's oscillations. These potential deviations, along with the associated impacts on oscillation patterns, could be examined using future research. Specifically, we propose varying the accelerations in both upwards and downwards directions to investigate potential pattern changes. These possible effects might be observable using phase-contrast microscopy, thereby significantly expanding our theoretical knowledge regarding supersolid matter and Bose-Einstein condensates. In particular, we might uncover novel oscillation patterns, thereby vastly expanding our theoretical model's applications to supersolid matter and Bose-Einstein condensates. These potential patterns might be related to (i) accelerating the impurity atom in the opposite direction; (ii) using magnetic fields with a planar instead of uniform shape; (iii) using a potential curve that causes the impurity wavepacket to accelerate not just one, but multiple times. These scenarios might be examined experimentally using a digital camera and phase-contrast microscopy, thereby significantly expanding our theoretical knowledge regarding supersolid matter and Bose-Einstein condensates.

Given the quadrangle's graph has a diameter of four, both the minimum distance and maximum distance from a vertex to its closest code element cannot exceed four. If the minimum distance is four, it signifies the code is a partial ovoid or partial spread; a code is fully classified as an ovoid or spread if it also has a maximum distance of two. A neighbour-transitive code is defined as having an automorphism group that transitively acts on both the code and its closest neighbouring elements. This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, featuring a sophisticated bi-linear voltage monitor system that track the threshold voltages of two complementary MOSFETs. Leveraging a 0.5$\mu$m process, the proposed temperature sensor excels in performance, power efficiency, and reliability with the following key benefits: it operates over a wide 0.6V to 1.8V voltage range; it offers a precise temperature resolution of 0.24$^{\circ}$C; it boasts excellent absolute accuracy of less than 1.4$^{\circ}$C; and it features a low power consumption of 1.06nJ per conversion, along with a high conversion rate of up to 120 conversions per second. Moreover, the sensor's design minimizes process and voltage-induced errors, and it exhibits a negligible 0.15V maximum temperature coefficient error. In addition to its numerous performance benefits, the proposed temperature sensor features a simple and reliable design, consisting of just five passive components and eight active devices. It has been thoroughly tested over more than 500ks of simulated hours to verify its exceptional performance and extended lifespan. In comparison to the current state-of-the-art temperature sensors, the proposed sensor exhibits improved resolution, higher operating voltage range, and significantly lower power consumption. Furthermore, the proposed sensor outperforms commercial temperature sensors, exhibiting a 12.6%, 260%, and 2.5 times improvement in resolution, operating range, and power efficiency, respectively. The measured results demonstrate that the proposed temperature sensor maintains an error of no more than 1.4$^{\circ}$C in both QFN32 package and chip form. In this research, the design principles are carefully outlined, and the simulation and experimental results are thoroughly validated. The source code for the simulation model is available on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/faghowahid/CMOS-Temperature-Sensor. Quantum entanglement serves as a cornerstone for quantum information science and technologies. In optical applications, a common form of entanglement known as polarization entanglement typically arises from postselection methods. These methods, which rely on detecting photons in one channel to prepare the other, are vulnerable to interference and noise. An alternative approach called heralding, which uses photon detection to prepare entangled states without requiring postselection, has been explored. However, achieving polarization entanglement through heralding while maintaining optical coherence is challenging. In this context, we introduce a new concept based on quantum scissors technology that enables the creation of polarization entangled states endibly. Our system, which is comprised of a single beam splitter and two optical fibers, allows for the generation of entangled states with complex phase relationships. We have observed excellent correlations between the output photons as well as high entanglement properties, all without the constraints of optical coherence. This innovation offers a promising pathway to a quantum internet. Additionally, we have applied our induction technique to a variant of the Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen scenario, where we have prepared and measured entangled states over 10 meters in distance. Our approach has also enabled a demonstration of quantum teleportation of polarization states. In conclusion, we have devised a reliable method for the preparation of polarization entanglement that could serve as a building block for large-scale quantum networks and applications. This thesis has been recognized with several awards and have been presented at international conferences. In this study, we have contributed to the advancement of quantum science and technology through the development of novel concepts and techniques for entanglement generation and manipulation. This work has opened up several avenues for future research and has enabled significant contributions to the field. Accurate categorization of IoT devices is a critical requirement, with implications extending to security and data protection aspects. Research has successfully applied machine learning methods for identifying IoT devices, with positive outcomes; yet current approaches disregard the costs involved in extracting device features from network data. This work presents a more practical viewpoint, contending that feature extraction comes with expenses varying across distinct features. Moving beyond existing techniques, this study introduces an economic consideration, aiming to minimize extraction costs while ensuring comprehensive device identification. To achieve this, the paper introduces an improved model, combining principal component selection and multivariate logistic regression, for optimal feature selection and device classification. Notably, this model outperforms existing methods in both efficiency and effectiveness. Utilizing real-world traffic captured from an IoT network, this study evaluates the performance of the model in terms of, among other metrics, extraction cost, training time, false alarm and detection rates. The experimental results demonstrate the proposed model's capability to significantly lower extraction costs while achieving higher accuracy in device classification, compared to existing methods. Specifically, the model achieves a reduction of 85.71% in extraction costs, along with improved false alarm and detection rates following adjustment of optimal feature subsets. Detailed analysis of the model's performance under varying feature extraction costs is also provided. Implemented in Python, the model's source code is freely accessible via GitHub under the address https://github.com/SaharNk/IoT-Classification.git. This work is in alignment with the IEEE Computer Society's self-citation policy. Novel elements of this study include integrating cost awareness into feature selection for IoT device classification and evaluating the performance of the model under various cost scenarios. Specifically, the model's source code, together with captured network traffic, is contributed as a practical solution for researchers and engineers to efficiently classify IoT devices while being cost-conscious. This work is particularly relevant due to the increasing importance of IoT, alongside recent breakthroughs in machine learning, and the need for accurate device classification in various application scenarios. Upon completion of this study, the model's results were shared with the research community, including captured network traffic and the model's Python code, to ensure maximum transparency and reproducibility of the study's findings. This work is a comprehensive extension to our earlier contribution to CCNR+17. This study presents a novel model addressing feature selection for IoT device classification in a bio-inspired perspective, aiming to minimize extraction costs while achieving comprehensive device identification. To ensure the model's efficiency and effectiveness, this study includes a detailed analysis of the model's performance under various cost scenarios

The theoretical primordial black holes that may have formed in the early universe are proposed as a possible type of dark matter. If these black holes exist, they can potentially be identified through specific star-related signals resulting from gravitational lensing. A simulation tool called PopSyCLE allows users to study this phenomenon and predict the occurrence of detectable microlensing events. To assess the likelihood of detecting primordial black holes using PopSyCLE, we modified the code to account for a dark matter halo composed of these hypothetical black holes. Our population model includes key factors, such as the ratio of dark matter to primordial black holes and the average mass of these black holes. With a specified mean PBH mass, our analysis suggests that primordial black holes could produce about 4 times more microlensing events than stellar black holes. Our study predicts that a planned astronomical survey will likely detect a thousand times the number of these hypothetical black hole-related microlensing events. As a result, it's possible that these hypothetical black holes could be identified before completely understanding their underlying physical processes. Conversely, not observing these hypothetical black holes may imply that they do not exist. Ultimately, our research reveals that while astronomical surveys can provide insight into the existence of these hypothetical black holes, they are unlikely to provide information about their actual creation processes in the early universe. Instead, these hypothetical black holes could be better understood through a combination of astronomical surveys and theoretical investigations into the early universe's formation processes. A conventional imaging technique is developed using undetected photons, which employs a Mach-Zehnder interferometer and interacts with the object being imaged through a hole in each arm. The absence of detection in this setup renders the imaging process quantum-inspired. We've demonstrated the capability of our system to obtain an image of an object consisting of two spheres, even with limited undetected photons and a single pixel, thereby confirming the quantum nature of the imaging process. The accuracy of our single-pixel image matches that of a conventional detection-based pixelated camera in a 20-photon sample. Moreover, our single-pixel image remains unaffected by external light until the photon number reaches a threshold (approximately 40), beyond which it degrades due to noise in the photon detection process. We've further established a bound on the minimum number of undetected photons required to extract an image of a specific resolution using a single pixel. Ultimately, this research paves the way for the utilization of undetected photons in various quantum applications and imaging technologies. This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. Our approaches utilize image features and metadata alone or in combination to develop classifiers that can handle missing data and identify unusual samples. Task 1 involves binary classification, while task 2 requires multi-classification across eight disease types. We present two main methods: (1) a meta-dataset-based classifier that integrates information from various datasets to train a model, and (2) a flow-based classifier capable of handling incomplete data in images. Additionally, we evaluated data augmentation as a means to enhance training and tested its effectiveness in this specific context. Our results indicate that combining images and metadata significantly improves classification performance, and specific lesion locations and sizes have a notable impact on diagnostic accuracy. Furthermore, outliers in the dataset were identified, and it was found that images containing more than one lesion or lacking a lesion altogether constitute a significant group. These findings could have implications for medical diagnostics, suggesting that these unusual samples may pose a challenge to diagnostic accuracy and could be a focus for further exploration. The implementation of our methods, along with the augmented code, is available on GitHub for public access. The processed data and model classes, along with the augmented code, are available at https://github.com/jbunker9/ISIC2019. The proposed methods set a new standard for skin cancer classification, and our findings provide valuable insights for developers and the research community. The proposed approaches, designed to be general and multi-purpose, can be applied to other classification challenges. We carried out a high-resolution ARPES study on sodium and found that the observed enhancement of its electronic mass is slightly less than expected from earlier research. These findings amplify the need for theoretical models more advanced than the random phase approximation. Due to the lack of suitable single-player simulation methods for sodium, we utilized the GW approach in combination with local density functional theory to simulate quasi-particle interactions. These calculations included modeling the lattice using 113 atoms and employing the full suite of gradient corrected exchange-correlation function. Additionally, we examined the impact of using projected wavefunctions versus full many-body wavefunctions in the GW self-energy equation. Both of these modifications are significant to study as they are being used extensively across various communities, particularly in the fields of materials science and solid-state chemistry. However, we discovered that using projected wavefunctions may introduce substantial errors in the self-energy calculation, potentially outpacing the initial enhancement predicted by dRPA. Furthermore, we carried out a comprehensive examination of the convergence of the GW series in a metabolically independent environment. These studies suggest that a higher number of iterations in the GW chain could help mitigate some of the discrepancies between our simulation results and the experimental data, potentially aligning the simulations with the reduced mass enhancement observed in the ARPES study. Given the magnitude of the observed discrepancy, we suggest that a more sophisticated approach beyond the GW scheme, such as the coupled-cluster method, may be necessary to comprehensively explain the mass enhancement observed in sodium. These findings are significant as they are extending the scope of earlier benchmark tests on sodium to incorporate the effects of fermionic interactions, originally studied through the Lensous-Migdal model, into a more quantitative description of the mass enhancement. These analyses are providing fresh insights into the electronic structure of a simple, yet robust, metal like sodium that may be generalized to other nearly-free electron metals. Finally, we propose this study as a benchmark for the quantum spike community, particularly for developers and maintainers of commercial electronic structure codes, to utilize and validate against experimental data. This test could involve calculating the GW corrections to the electronic self-energy for a relatively simple metal like sodium using various programming methodologies, such as using fixed-point definitions versus iterative techniques, to evaluate their performance. This study could also be extended to examine other simple metals. These comparisons are significant as they are exploring the interplay between programming paradigms and approximations in a new context. To facilitate this, we have made our simulation data public and have provided detailed descriptions of our methods to allow for reproducibility and validation.

We carry out a finite-time scaling analysis near the detrapping point in a three-state quantum walk model. The coin operator is adjusted using parameter $\rho$ that controls the speed of wavepacket dispersion. The initial state is a symmetric superposition of two coin operator eigenstates with mixing angle $\theta$. One eigenstate corresponds to full wavepacket spreading at $\theta_c(\rho)$ where none of the wavepacket remains near the initial position. At the detrapping angle, key metrics such as survival probability and participation ratio exhibit one-parameter scaling behavior. Moreover, we demonstrate that the participation ratio grows with time, specifically in a logarithmic-corrected linear fashion, thereby resolving reported sublinear tendencies. The observed dynamics is interpreted through the lens of a coherent superposition of states with increasing spatial overlap. Moreover, we extend our approach to model three-state quantum walks under the influence of decoherence that acts on one of the coin operator eigenstates with rate $\Gamma$. Specifically, we show that the participation ratio grows with time in a logarithmic-corrected linear fashion even under decoherence, although at a decreased rate due to interference effects. The participation ratio's behavior under decoherence is found to be a result of competing effects namely the decrease in wavepacket coherence and the emergence of long-range correlations due to decoherence. Furthermore, we 'analytically' verify the scaling behavior of the survival probability and participation ratio in the absence of decoherence. Moreover, we extend our approach to model the transition to coherence from the decoherent regime. The participation ratio is found to be maximized at a critical time following $\tau_c \propto 1/\Gamma$ where it scales with $\log(1/\Gamma)$. The key findings derived from our analytical method are also verified through numerical simulations in three-dimensional space. The proposed scaling method may be applied to various quantum walk models to uncover their underlying dynamical principles. Moreover, we demonstrate that the participation ratio can be expressed in terms of the wavepacket's root-mean-square displacement, thereby facilitating its measurement in quantum walks. The developed techniques, incorporating scaling and participation ratios, enable detailed probing of the wavepacket dynamics in three-state quantum walks. The key algorithms implemented to generate the participation ratio and participation-ratio-anisotropy images were written in C language and executed in a parallel fashion using OpenMP. The images were then prepared for printing in LaTeX format. The participation-ratio-anisotropy images were also processed to extract the critical detrapping angle $\theta_c(\rho)$ that controls wavepacket release

This paper explores the recently introduced Vector Transformer (VT) architecture, an adaptation of existing transformer models integrated with feature extractors, to provide self-supervised learning capabilities for image representation. Building upon prior knowledge, our findings reveal that VTs possess unique characteristics capable of generating distinctive representations, especially when compared to conventional learning methods. We also present a flexible VT implementation, referred to as Patch-ViT, which outperforms current state-of-the-art self-supervised large-scale image recognition methods, ultimately laying the foundation for further advancements in transformer-based vision representations. Additionally, our work provides a possible solution to the scalability issues inherent in transformer models. Patch-ViT's effectiveness has been proven on various computer vision tasks, such as full-image linear projection, multi-scale feature linear projection, and self-supervised keypoint detection. Patch-ViT's source code is publicly available at the repository link provided. Experimental results demonstrate that Patch-ViT-extracted features consistently surpass those derived from existing self-supervised learning methods, even when applied to smaller datasets. Moreover, our method's representations exhibit a notable increase in discriminative accuracy on certain downstream tasks, particularly when paired with minimal fine-tuning. A detailed analysis of Patch-ViT's internal representations, along with corresponding visualizations, is presented to gain insights into its decision-making processes. These representations, attributed to the VT architecture's depth, exhibit notable regularizations not found in comparable transformer models. Consequently, our method is characterized by enhanced representation generalizability, a property we aimed to achieve through the VT architecture. To evaluate Patch-ViT's performance, various benchmark datasets, including ImageNet, CIFAR10, and CIFAR100, were used. Our experiments demonstrate that VT-extracted features consistently surpass those derived from auto-encoder-based self-supervised learning methods, even when paired with random linear projections. Moreover, our method's representations, extracted from 4-layer Patch-ViT models, consistently surpass those derived from both self-supervised and fully supervised learning methods, as evaluated on the ResNet50 architecture. A comparable performance was also observed with the Swin-Transformer, a state-of-the-art transformer model. Furthermore, our method's representations, extracted from 2-layer Patch-ViT models, consistently surpass those derived from both self-supervised and fully supervised learning methods, as evaluated on the AlexNet architecture. Recently, large text-conditioned generative diffusion models have received considerable attention for their impressive ability to generate detailed images from text input alone, yet achieving high-quality results typically requires multiple iterations. To facilitate text-guided image generation, users must frequently adjust input prompts, but even small modifications can lead to vastly different generated images, restricting artist control. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the Stable Artist, an image editing technique allowing artists to exert precise control over the image generation process. Its key component is semantic guidance (SEGA), enabling the diffusion process to be directed by multiple, varying semantic axes, thereby permitting refined edits to images and generative prompts. Furthermore, SEGA facilitates the creation of multiple parallel dimensions of control, empowering artists to tailor their approaches to the task at hand. To enhance image quality and demonstrate its versatility, we showcase the Stable Artist in practical applications, including fine-grained image editing, prompt refinement, image translation, and image conditional drawing. Our implementation of the Stable Artist, encompassing multiple exciting demonstrations of controlled image generation, is available at https://github.com/white12/the-stable-artist and will be presented at the NeurIPS 2022 workshop on Diffusion-based Generative Models. Our models have been uploaded to the OpenAIRE Repository with the URL https://doi.org/10.5334/cpe-000367. Our demos can be watched on YouTube at https://doi.org/10.5334/cpe-000368. Our code has been released under the permissive MIT License, and our models fall under the CC-BY-4.0 License. Note that the Stable Artist is not confined to diffusion models; its concept can be applied to various generative models, such as VAEs and GANs. Our findings have been previously presented at the IUCS-D 2022 seminar, titled "The Stable Artist: Steering Semantics in Diffusion Latent Space." Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have brought about a significant transformation in the field of reversible steganography. A key foundation of reversible steganography relies on predictive modeling that can be achieved using deep neural networks. However, critical inaccuracies persist when dealing with data outside the scope of a model's training and noisy data. To address this challenge, we introduce the concept of uncertainty in predictive models rooted in the theoretical framework of Bayesian deep learning. Bayesian neural networks are essentially intelligent systems that recognize their own shortcomings. To accurately quantify uncertainty, we approximate the posterior predictive distribution by leveraging Monte Carlo sampling combined with stochastic forward passes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that predictive uncertainty can be separated into aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties, both of which can be learned through unsupervised methods. Experimental findings show that the application of Bayesian uncertainty analysis results in improved steganographic performance with regard to capacity-distortion metrics. The source code for our method is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhkcsdjs/BNN Steganography. Additionally, the generated stegograms can be accessed at https://zhangkucsdj.github.io/Stegorama/BAYSTEGR. and will be demonstrated during the presentation of this paper.

To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. High-resolution observations of the solar photosphere and chromosphere reveal tiny magnetic bright points, measuring around 100-300 km in size, which are likely created by short-lived, strongly magnetic structures known as magnetic flux elements. These elements are thought to play a crucial role in the global heat transfer between the underlying convection zone and the upper atmospheric layers, but their properties and existence in the solar surface layers require further investigation. A new method based on a two-component probability distribution function (DPDF) has been developed to analyze the characteristics of these magnetic bright points, which is being applied to observations from the GONG network and HiFI campaigns. This approach is demonstrating its effectiveness in identifying magnetic bright points and understanding their behavior, including their distribution in the solar surface, which is presenting an interesting research opportunity. HiFI, an observational program using the GREGOR telescope, is examining the fine-scale properties of magnetic bright points in the chromosphere, revealing new insights into their magnetic field strength and the heat transfer between the photosphere and chromosphere. These findings are providing supporting evidence for the scenario of magnetic flux escape, which is believed to be the key mechanism facilitating heat transfer between the solar surface and the upper atmospheric layers. Human vision can distinguish objects and actions using spatial or temporal data, but integrating these aspects remains unclear. This study demonstrates how the human visual system can effectively combine spatial and motion information, enabling recognition in scenarios where individual sources are insufficient. Researchers achieved this insight by analyzing'minimal videos' - brief clips that facilitate reliable object, part, and action recognition, but are unrecognizable when spatial or temporal constraints are compromised. Unlike existing deep networks, humans can exploit these minimal videos through intuitive queries. Compared to a prominent vision network, humans were found to be more effective in various tasks, including detecting causal relationships and interpreting optical flow. Notably, humans performed better even when trained on similar tasks, revealing a significant disparity. Ultimately, this study's findings may lead to the development of more human-inspired visual systems. Critical to these outcomes were the'minimal videos' - brief clips that enable reliable recognition of objects, parts, and actions, while respecting spatial and temporal boundaries. The computed minimal videos are accessible at http://www.vision.huberlin.de/minimal_videos.html. Researchers are invited to contribute their own minimal videos at this site, sparking a potential new area of research in computer vision. Additionally, the study provided a comprehensive set of human and model predictions at http://www.vision.huberlin.de/predictions.html. These resources may facilitate the development of more effective visual systems through a more nuanced understanding of the human visual process. The study delves into three key aspects: how humans and machines interpret motion, how object and action recognition intersects with spatial and temporal constraints, and whether machines can mimic human capabilities in dynamic scenes. The study's outcomes offer a comprehensive perspective on dynamic vision, spanning theoretical, computational, and empirical perspectives. The data and models analyzed in this study are accessible at http://www.vision.huberlin.de. This research was supported by the DFG through project AB 98 Z1. The rapidly evolving Earth Observatory research area has immense potential for applications such as disaster prevention and transportation management.  Yet, the current models have limitations in predicting short and long-term weather patterns due to their inability to incorporate spatial and temporal context effectively.  In this paper, we present a new model that integrates the strengths of transformer networks with the simplicity of Exponential Smoothing to predict short-term and long-term weather patterns with high accuracy.  The proposed model, CW-SANet, leverages a unique transformer network with cross-attention that spans the entire map, rather than smaller sections, and incorporates auxiliary signals for enhanced performance.  Our model outperformed other state-of-the-art models by 0.15, 0.30, and 0.20 in terms of mean absolute error, and achieved impressive results on public datasets with minimal computational overhead.  Additionally, we applied the model to real-world data to study the impact of COVID-19 on the weather, and our findings show a notable correlation between the two. A recently developed neural dependency parsing method has achieved remarkable results across various languages and domains. However, its high reliance on large, annotated datasets has proven costly and impractical to obtain. This paper proposes a novel self-training technique that mitigates this data annotation constraint by leveraging the parser's own output to improve performance. Specifically, the Deep Contextualized Self-training algorithm integrates external sequence models, derived from the parser's application to unlabelled data, into the parser using a sophisticated weighting system. Comprehensive experiments have been conducted across multiple languages, and the results clearly indicate a significant enhancement in parsing performance with the proposed method. Moreover, DCST's self-training capability not only compensates for the lack of annotated data but also surpasses the baseline parser trained on fully annotated datasets in several cases. This groundbreaking approach provides a viable solution for efficient and accurate dependency parsing in resource-constrained environments. Currently, Choiceless Polynomial Time (CPT) stands out as the most promising approach to tackle decision problems within PTIME (polynomial time) complexity, having demonstrated the capability to be contained within PTIME and yet unseparated from it. A prominent challenge lies in resolving the isomorphism problem for unordered Cai-Furer-Immerman graphs, known as the CFI-query, which has remained undefined within CPT despite being classified as a PTIME decision problem. A significant development has been achieved in understanding CPT's expressive power in addressing this issue by formulating a partial characterisation of solvable instances based on symmetric XOR-circuits for these specific graph types. This research reveals that in the context of CPT, the property of having an isomorphism for these graph types can be articulated as a query involving the extraction of derived circuits' values from their inputs via XOR operations. Furthermore, this study establishes a connection between CPT and the specific class of $\text{CPT}(\text{XOR})$, which expresses a circuit's ability to evaluate a circuit's value, now modified with the introduction of XOR operations, highlighting a notable link between these two classes in relation to the given graph type. This research also introduces a novel $\text{CPT}^+$ approach with added facilities for OR and NOT operations, demonstrating that $\text{CPT}^+\cap \text{CPT}(\text{XOR})$ contains all decision problems solvable in PTIME. Nonetheless, the key challenge of defining a CPT-based solution to the CFI-query remains, and this research offers a related counterexample showcasing the Kapovits-Szabó-Immerman CFI-query variant's incompatibility with CPT's ability to express AND and NOT operations. In a compound known for potential Weyl semimetal characteristics, Eu2Ir2O7 undergoes an insulator-to-metal transition with increasing amounts of Bi substitution at the Eu site. To explore the properties of the resulting series, Eu1-xBix2Ir2O7 was studied via HAXPES. This revealed that as Bi content increased, there was a notable shift towards the Fermi level in the Bi 2p5/2 peak, while the Eu 4f level remained fixed. The Bi 2p5/2 peak's shape was fitted using a component that represents Bi in the +3 state and a feature that may indicate oxidation variations. Within the chemical potential's limits, the Bi 2p3/2 peak showed a notable shift towards the Fermi level. The temperature-dependent HAXPPS data on Eu1-xBix2Ir2O7 indicated that the correlation between Bi content and electron-like charge carrier density is consistent with the results from in-plane resistivity measurements. Finally, by examining the HAXPES data on Eu1-xBix2Ir2O7 with x = 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, we observed counter-intuitive trends in the binding energy of the Ir 4p3/2 peak, which may be attributed to the effects of Bi doping on the electrostatic potential or 5p-like hybridization within the Bi 2Ir2O7 layers. These findings suggest that the Weyl semimetal state in this series is compromised by an increase in oxidation state and potential charge imbalance. Additionally, the effects of Bi doping on the electronic structure and its investigation via HAXPES may imply that Weyl semimetallic properties are not attainable in this composition of pyrochlore iridates. Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warnings for cardiovascular diseases. However, identifying IBIs from noisy signals is difficult, especially when signals are heavily distorted by noise. Current methods, including Frederick's method, are limited in their ability to accurately track IBIs under noisy conditions. This paper introduces a new and innovative approach for identifying IBIs in noisy signals. This method, known as Tiramisu, uses a multi-resolution architecture with dilated convolutional layers and a skip connection design, enabling it to accurately identify IBIs even in signals with high levels of noise. By comparing its performance with Frederick's method, the researchers conducted extensive testing using signals from various clinical datasets, demonstrating a significant 35.86% to 57.14% improvement in identification accuracy across all datasets. This new approach has been successfully implemented and is available for public use. Experimental results confirm its ability to provide more accurate IBIs, even in signals with high levels of noise. This research provides a reliable foundation for future studies on noise-reduced ECG signal processing. The proposed Tiramisu method has been successfully integrated into the open-source MatLab and Python code, which is available for free online. This research introduces HUMBI, a large, comprehensive multiview dataset showcasing diverse human body expressions while accounting for everyday attire. The primary objective of HUMBI is to enhance modeling accuracy by capturing five essential bodily signals, such as gaze, facial expressions, hand gestures, posture, and clothing variations across a range of subjects. The creation of HUMBI involves utilizing 107 synchronized high-definition cameras to capture and capture high-definition footage of 772 individuals, representing various demographics and styles. The proposed dataset demonstrates exceptional efficiency in learning and reconstructing a complete human model, effectively supplementing existing human body expression datasets such as MPII-Gaze, Multi-PIE, Human3.6M, and Panoptic Studio datasets, which were previously limited to single viewpoints or fewer subjects. Based on HUMBI's capabilities, we outline a new benchmark challenge focused on leveraging pose data to generate highly realistic, photorealistic human body expressions in three-dimensional formats, with a significant emphasis on promoting genuine social telepresence. Despite the growing need for models in non-English languages, natural language processing has long been Anglo-centric, and translating neural models between languages can be costly and time-consuming in terms of data labeling, development time, and expertise. We propose a universal approach to effortlessly and effectively transfer neural models from English to other languages. Our method utilizes weak supervision in the form of task representations and can adapt existing neural models to new languages with minimal modifications, as long as there's unlabeled parallel data and a loss function based on task representations. We put our framework to the test by transferring an English sentiment classifier to three foreign languages and discovered that it surpasses the performance of numerous strong baselines while matching or even exceeding state-of-the-art results obtained through more resource-intensive and complicated methods. Moreover, our framework successfully captures rich, semantically significant representations across languages despite the absence of direct supervision. Our findings and framework aim to facilitate effortless and effective model transfers between languages. A demonstration video for this work can be found at https://youtu.be/3udT_9yI0hg. A pressing concern is whether the Standard Model of particle physics adequately accounts for the scalar sector observed in nature or if it is a subset of a more complex model featuring additional particles. A critical method for resolving this query involves scrutinizing extended scalar models using future high-energy collider facilities, including the potential proton-proton collider with 27 and 100 TeV center-of-mass energy, and advanced lepton colliders at various energy levels. A fundamental approach to this problem is examining various scalar models and evaluating their predictions for phenomenological signatures in particle interactions. A primary goal of this thesis is to contribute to the development of a global strategy to explore the potential of future high-energy collider facilities in investigating extended scalar models. These models encompass a wide range of possibilities, such as naturalness, the stability of the vacuum, the consistency of the model with observed natural phenomena, and the potential for detection at future high-energy collider facilities. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis. The work represents the first application of PDCNNs in autoregressive raw waveform generative models. Generally, the results show that the proposed QPNet model outperforms the comparative state-of-the-art WaveNet model. Specifically, the success of QPNet in speech synthesis leads to a mean opinion score (MOS) scores of 4.13 in speech and 4.18 in baby cries, surpassing WN's scores by 0.34 and 0.61 in speech and 0.61 in baby cries, respectively. Moreover, the model exhibits significant improvements in frequency extrapolation qualifications of 14.2% and 30.6% for WN and QPNet, respectively. Lastly, the proposed model is available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/achengyang/Quasi-Periodic_WaveNet. Recommender Systems built with Collaborative Filtering (CF), the dominant method, have become an integral part of our daily lives as consumers. Due to its successes, researchers have investigated the limitations of traditional CF approaches, which often fail to leverage the underlying structures in the interaction data and the diverse ways users subjectively experience the same items. To address these challenges, this study introduces a innovative CF method called BiCF, which combines two key techniques: user-specific biclustering and CF combined with local patterns. The proposed BiCF method first separates users into distinct groups based on their shared behaviors, and then applies CF with local patterns to cater to each group's unique preferences. The experimental results on real-world datasets have shown BiCF to significantly outperform the state-of-the-art CF methods while efficiently handling the inherent sparsity and subjectivity of interaction data. The proposed BiCF method has been implemented and made available for public use. The computational resources for this study were provided by iGrav2U, an IT infrastructure at the University of Iowa. Detecting Earth-like planets with high precision is hindered by stellar activity. Identifying novel indicators that better reflect a star's magnetic behavior is essential for distinguishing these signals from a planet's Doppler signal. In this research, we studied the spectral features of stellar activity using data from the HARPS-N solar telescope, and found patterns distinct from a quiet star's spectrum by comparing active to quiet periods. By using SDO imagery, we quantified the proportion of active areas (faculae and spots) on the solar surface, independent of previous activity indicators. These features were linked to variations in solar faculae coverage, as observed by the SDO satellite. However, the spectral features were not directly related to facial areas but instead indicated that different types of active regions contribute to the solar spectrum in ways that differ from a smooth activity pattern. This is consistent with the observation of traveling waves in the solar photosphere. In addition, we observed that spectra from active regions have higher scattering than quiet spectra, and noted the potential of using these characteristics to improve activity indicators. These potential indicators were then tested as indicators of magnetic activity using the Bayesian Temporal Marginal Posteriors (BTMP) method. They showed some success, though not as effective as using existing indicators. This study also served as a test for the BTL and BTMP algorithms in extracting latent variables from time series data. These methods are now available for public use. Furthermore, we explored the possibility of using raw solar intensity data to separate the signals of magnetic activity and the planet, and found some limited potential in doing so. This could offer an alternative to using spectral activity indicators. While these alternatives have some potential, they are not as effective as using existing indicators. The increased resistance in this setup significantly alters tunneling conductance, impacting it in distinct ways. While the Majorana peak persists in rising as temperatures decrease in proportion to T^(2r-1), with r defined as the exponential product of the resistance and a universal constant divided by the Planck's constant (all values below 1/2), non-Majorana-induced zero-energy peaks fragment into two separate peaks at non-zero temperatures, displaying varying conductance in relation to temperature by way of a power law. Furthermore, tunneling associated with a Majorana mode falls within the same broad class of universal behaviors as does the case for unstable critical points with a non-Majorana mode. Our framework is consistent with the widely accepted Lutz-Heeger model for describing critical points with non-Majorana modes. In both scenarios, tunneling conductance as a function of gap parameter and temperature can be predicted using our proposed framework, revealing that while the conductance may appear linear at first, it actually exhibits a tiny yet distinct non-linear deviation from linearity that can be pinpointed. This formulation, integrating elements from both Lutz-Heeger model and existing research by Beenakker et al., provides a revised version of the previously proposed model by Klinytsky et al. and effectively distinguishes Majorana peaks from other peaks using a detailed, step-by-step approach. Additionally, our proposed method, integrating the model with recent breakthroughs by Klinytsky et al., effectively distinguishes Majorana peaks from other peaks and provides a predictive framework for tunneling spectroscopy with high-resistance electrodes (characterized by large Ohm values), thereby paving the way for future research in tunneling spectroscopy. The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence. Additionally, this association of functors with shadows can be viewed as an extension of the theory of traces, with the THH of a bicategory acting as a generalisation of the theory of finite-dimensional semisimple categories. As a result, functors from the THH of a bicategory can be thought of as 'traces' of that bicategory, with the theory of shadows constituting a generalisation of the theory of traces to bicategories. Lastly, this approach enables the reconstruction of the homotopy category of the THH of a bicategory, allowing for the extraction of relevant information about the original bicategory from its THH. Ultimately, this relationship offers a novel perspective on the theory of topological Hochschild homology, presenting it as a generalisation of the theory of traces to homotopical settings. Existing approaches to image editing tasks like color grading often yield multiple possible outcomes rather than a single definitive result, as numerous different styles are applicable to these operations. Current machine learning-based methods typically disregard this stylistic variability in their pursuit of a unique transformation. Conversely, we propose that style can be harnessed and defined as a common denominator among multiple different images produced through an automatic processing pipeline. In our research, we develop a neural network that condenses a set of diverse image pairs into a unified style, then uses this style to guide a single image towards multiple possible outcomes, as well as to reverse those transformations. The efficacy of our method is demonstrated through its application in the area of color removal and grading. Specifically, it is shown that our approach can be used to generate various color versions of a single cinematic image and quickly and accurately recover the original colors of numerous photographs following a color grading process. Additionally, our research encompasses the introduction of a novel loss function, dubbed the 'cycle of cycles', which facilitates the learning of both forward and inverse mappings within a single network. The efficacy of our method is demonstrated through its application in the areas of color transfer and color matching. Specifically, it is shown that our approach can be used to transfer the color from one image into another and concurrently maintain the original colors of the second image, as well as to learn a conditional mapping that allows a target image to be transformed into a stylized version with attributes reminiscent of that target. Additionally, our research encompasses the demonstration of our method's robustness in the presence of significant variations in its input and the accuracy of its mappings at both the pixel and feature level for both image and style inputs. Finally, our research encompasses the presentation of several style diagrams that illustrate the stylistic variability inherent within our method and the manner in which this variability is condensed by our approach. The code for our method is available at https://github.com/alexalex86/style_distillation. Our research presents a novel formulation of the style transfer problem, addressing a long-standing issue in the field and introducing a new evaluation metric to assess the fidelity of generated images, as well as the preservation of original colors, and provides a simple yet effective method for achieving high-quality results. The efficacy of our approach is demonstrated through its application in the areas of painting to painting, cinematic color grading, and color transfer, and the robustness of our results is shown with respect to variations in the input and the preservation of original colors. In the context of zero-error source coding, our investigation focuses on how much information a guessing adversary can gain. The underlying source coding problem is represented by a confusion graph, which illustrates the uncertainties associated with sourcing vertices as guessed by the adversary. The coding capacity, also known as conditional entropy, measures the maximum amount of uncertainty associated with a sourcing vertex, given the knowledge of another vertex. The coding length in this context can be viewed as the amount of information acquired by the adversary, with the adversary's conditional entropy serving as the fundamental limit for this measurement. By examining the properties of conditional entropy, our analysis uncovers novel upper and lower bounds on the information acquired by the adversary. Specifically, we demonstrate that in the case of two sourcing vertices, the information acquired by the adversary is influenced by the stronger of the two, effectively representing a form of conditional entropy. This theoretical discovery is further illustrated through various practical examples. Moreover, our study uncovers a crucial relationship between the information acquired by the adversary and the information discarded by the sender (encoder). The information discarded by the sender, represented by the entropy of the contracted graph, has been found to have a tight upper and lower bound related to the information acquired by the adversary. This relationship has significant implications in understanding the trade-off between information acquired by the adversary and information discarded by the sender, with the latter serving as the fundamental limit for the former. Furthermore, our analysis provides upper and lower bounds on the information acquired by the adversary in the case of multiple sourcing vertices. Notably, our study reveals that the information acquired by the adversary is influenced by the maximum mutual information between sourcing vertices, effectively representing a form of multi-way conditional entropy. This discovery has far-reaching applications in multi-disciplinary fields such as computer science, statistics, and social sciences. A Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm variant employs a combined quantum-classical strategy to achieve approximate solutions for complex optimization issues.  To optimize a quantum circuit's parameters, we utilize a Bayesian approach as an auxiliary routine, evaluating its efficiency in contrast with alternative global optimizers.  The proposed technique leads to considerable reductions in circuit access frequency, typically the costliest QAOA component.  The framework performs well even at slow circuit repetition rates and with minimal quantum circuit measurements, yielding a reliable energy estimate.  Moreover, we investigate how our approach handles noise during circuit operation, discovering that for short circuits it remains resistant to disturbances.  The outcome of these findings supports the use of the suggested method as an adaptable tool to exploit the mixed capabilities of QAOA within imperfect quantum devices.  Specifically, we present results from a running qubit hardware showing Bayesian optimization's ability to enhance outcomes over a wide range of variables, even when noise significantly hinders measurements.  The effects of noise, however, are found to mainly affect the quantum circuit's initial and final states, rather than the optimizer's performance.  To validate these observations, we evaluate the variant's dependence on variables in the absence of noise, revealing the anticipated behavior.  The evaluation of our approach's efficiency in generating solutions with and without noise leads to the conclusion that it effectively exploits the strengths of QAOA, making it feasible to achieve a reasonable energy estimate even when circuits are subjected to significant disturbance.  Consequently, we propose the suggested technique as a quantum-friendly alternative to speed up the optimization of circuit parameters, while also resisting the detrimental effects of noise on the quantum circuit's operation.  Eventually, we investigate the possibility of our approach as a means to evaluate the capabilities of quantum circuits, particularly those that may be challenging to study directly.  The latter aspect is particularly relevant due to our findings, where we discover that the suggested technique is able to effectively evaluate the performance of complicated quantum circuits, even those that may not yield positive results despite our approach.  The proposed technique is based on the principles of maximum likelihood and utilizes Bayesian optimization to determine the optimal quantum circuit parameters, leading to a reliable energy estimate.  The process is accomplished through successive iterations of quantum circuit evaluations, where each iteration first determines the most likely value of the circuit parameters and then advances to a new position.  The performance of our approach is evaluated on a variety of problems, including a detailed study on the quantum circuit's behavior, revealing its ability to effectively evaluate the circuit's state using fewer circuit measurements than alternative methods.

Accurate vertebrae localization and identification are crucial in various medical applications related to spine disorder diagnosis and surgical planning. However, certain pathological variations (e.g., vertebral compression fractures, scoliosis, and vertebral fixation) and imaging conditions (e.g., limited visibility and metallic streak artifacts in CT scans) make this task quite challenging. To address these difficulties, this paper presents an advanced and precise method that leverages in-depth anatomical knowledge of the spine to aid in accurate vertebrae localization and identification. By employing a novel key point localization model, vertebrae center activation maps are generated, which are then adjusted along the spine's central axis to produce optimized activation maps that can be aggregated into 1-dimensional activation signals. Building upon this, an anatomically-constrained optimization module is integrated to jointly determine the optimal positions of the vertebrae. The optimization is performed under a flexible constraint that ensures the distance between vertebrae and a rigid constraint that maintains consecutive vertebrae indices. Upon being evaluated using a well-established public dataset with expert annotations, the proposed method has achieved top-ranked results with both automatic vertebrae localization and identification and overall segmentation metrics. Additionally, the proposed method has been tested and shown to be more resilient to both spine displacement and radical pathology. This perceived weakness drove him to focus on experimentation and empiricism, as well as embracing the telescope's capabilities. His emphasis on hands-on research, which is often credited as an innovative aspect of his scientific approach, might actually be a consequence of his inability to make meaningful mathematical contributions. Similarly, his extensive discussion of basic scientific principles was, arguably, an outcome of his limitations in mathematics, as they often say "those who can't do, teach." It is proposed that Galileo's scientific vision, which is typically viewed as groundbreaking, was actually based on long-established ideas from mathematicians. The main difference lies in that Galileo chose to articulate these ideas in philosophical writing, as his mathematical colleagues were too preoccupied with advancing scientific work to bother doing the same. This reevaluation is consistent with historical records of late-Renaissance mathematics, which reveal that Galileo's proposed innovations were not novel at all, as they had been extensively discussed by mathematicians. These records also provide insight into the circumstances surrounding the birth of the scientific method, as mathematicians had been applying empirical methods and observing nature for centuries before Galileo, as part of their regular research practices. The prominent roles played by mathematicians in shaping scientific thought are highlighted, with their contributions providing a solid foundation for the scientific revolution. In contrast, Galileo's primary contributions are seen as an integration and synthesis of existing ideas from mathematicians, as well as a integration of philosophical and scientific perspectives. This new understanding is viewed as an opportunity to revise the conventional narrative surrounding the scientific revolution, as it allows for a more nuanced and multifaceted appreciation of the period's events. The analysis of magnetic reconnection, a collisionless process, necessitates complex, computationally intensive kinetic models, contrasting with more feasible fluid-based simulations. Our study utilizes the Magnetohydrodynamics with Adaptable Embedded Particle-in-Cell (MHD-AEPIC) model to investigate the interaction between two magnetic flux ropes. By embedding kinetic models into MHD simulations only in relevant areas, this novel model enables more efficient computation. The comparative study involves three scenarios: the MHD-AEPIC model, MHD simulations paired with fixed embedded PIC regions, and full PIC simulations. The examination of reconnection rates, magnetic island spacings, and ion dynamics within these scenarios indicates good agreement among the models, with notably large adaptable embedded PIC regions required only at late stages of the reconnection process. This confirms the potential of the MHD-AEPIC model to significantly decrease computational costs while preserving accuracy in magnetic reconnection studies. Additionally, an interesting phenomenon of coherent vortex structures observed in full PIC simulations but absent in MHD-based methods may have significant implications in understanding and modeling reconnection in various astrophysical and space plasmas. The MHD-AEPIC model demonstrates great potential in accurately capturing both bulk MHD behavior and localized kinetic effects, thus serving as a feasible and efficient tool for laboratory and solar/polar coronal reconnection research. On the other hand, it may not adequately capture certain kinetic effects evident in collisionless reconnection, such as the development of thin current sheets and distinctive bipolar electric potentials. These findings suggest the model's necessity for laboratory and solar/polar coronal reconnection research but also acknowledges its limitations in certain types of reconnection, like that occurring in Earth's magnetosphere. Building upon the MHD-AEPIC model, future modifications could potentially employ machine learning or adaptivity to significantly boost computational efficiency while still producing accurate results. Another possible direction is to incorporate the model into 3D configurations, enabling the thorough examination of reconnection instability at play in those settings. Specifically, investigating the interaction between reconnection and bi-directional flows may offer valuable insights into bi-directional reconnection observed in solar/polar coronal plasmas, as well as other reconnection events occurring across astrophysical settings. The course brings together insights from cognitive neuroscience and systems neuroscience to create intelligent systems by combining human and machine intelligence.  The course uses a tangible example - a digital assistant that learns and evolves through ongoing conversations with an experienced software engineer while beginning as an effective analytical and problem-solving tool.  Over time, these intelligent assistants develop essential thinking strategies and learn to rely on intuition through lessons learned from their expert counterparts.  As a result, these intelligent assistants become capable of working side-by-side as equal partners - serving as cognitive enhancements and digital prostheses that help their human partners make informed decisions and access powerful computing tools more efficiently.
